Name: Babaco
Description:
Babaco fruits are spectacular fruits that deserve more recognition!
Although they are still mainly consumed in central and South America where they originated (we source ours from Ecuador), the mouthwatering taste of these hybrid fruits - they were created by combining two varieties of papaya (also known as pawpaw) - has enticed fruit lovers from across the world to enjoy their delicious flesh.
They have a unique shape, almost resembling an oblong but with 5 flat sides, cutting into appealing star-shaped slices, and a relatively large size, measuring up to 12 inches long and weighing up to 1.5kg! Once the fruit is fully ripened, babaco's thin, smooth skin takes on an attractive golden-yellow hue, and it is edible too! Underneath the skin is juicy white, seedless flesh that delights the tastebuds: the flavour is multi-layered and distinctive, with both sweet and acidic elements, but eaters distinguish notes of pineapple, kiwi, and its parent fruit papaya. What really makes the flesh stand out is its surprising fizziness - so renowned has this quality become that babaco has gained the nickname 'champagne fruit'!
Delectable when eaten fresh out of hand - remember the entire fruit is edible! - especially when sprinkled lightly with sugar, babaco's versatility means it can also be used in any number of sweet and savoury recipes. We'd recommend pureeing the flesh to create refreshing smoothies or tangy barbecue sauce (simply combine it with brown sugar, wine vinegar, ketchup, pepper, salt or soy sauce, and garlic), optimising its tropical flavour to make wonderful desserts, from pies to ice creams, and mix into salads. Babaco's relation to its parent fruit means it can additionally be utilised in any recipe calling for papaya. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recommended recipes, including a superb banana tiramisu, the ultimate dessert for fruit lovers!
As well as being extremely flavourful, babaco boasts many nutritional benefits too. In particular, babaco is an excellent source of vitamins A and C and is known to promote healthy digestion.

Name: Banana - banana leaves
Description:
In regions where bananas are cultivated, fresh banana leaves have many purposes.
Large, flexible, and waterproof, they are particularly useful during the cooking process: whether curries, rice, or vegetables, food is commonly wrapped and then steamed, grilled, or baked in these bright green leaves, because not only are they convenient, but the leaves also impart a delightfully fruity aroma and a certain freshness to the food it covers. The popular Indian snack paneer bhapa (check out the 'Further information' tab below for a recipe!) is a particularly excellent example of this, as the banana leaves provide it with an incomparable tropical flavour.
Banana leaves are used as plates too, and can even be BBQ mats. Simply place a piece of banana leaf on your BBQ, put your food on it, and cook! The leaf will turn bright green and then brown, infusing your food with a unique, sweet flavour.
Our fresh banana leaves are also ideal for decoration, adding a visually striking feature to any room, and are the perfect quirky gift for fruit fanatics.
In fact, we also sell whole banana leaves with stems that have become popular with food photographers! These full-length banana leaves (measuring about 2m in length) are carefully cut from by our supplier in Sri Lanka, who then packs the leaves in extra long boxes to ensure they safely reach us here in the UK. As well as being common sights in photoshoots, they are ideal centrepieces during celebrations too, often being used as a large platter to serve food on! If you're interested in acquiring full-length banana leaves with stems (which are very hard to find in the UK!) please email us on info@myexoticfruit.com.

Name: Banana - kolikuttu
Description:
Looking for a new banana variety to try? Kolikuttu bananas are just the thing for you!
Although small in size - they are roughly the same size as apple bananas, which are about half the length of Cavendish bananas - these plump 'baby bananas' are far superior to supermarket-bought bananas in aroma, texture, and flavour!
When you peel back the thin, smooth, yellow skin of kolikuttu bananas, you are instantly greeted with a glorious fragrance reminiscent of apples. Your tastebuds will be wowed by the cream-coloured flesh which is divinely soft (indeed, they are also known as 'silk bananas' due to their texture!) and has a perfectly balanced sweet-sour taste profile, with apple-like undertones. This creaminess and brilliant flavour have made them one of the most highly prized dessert banana varieties across Asia! Indeed, they are so highly regarded that they are one of the most commonly chosen fruits for offerings during religious festivals.
Delectable when eaten fresh out of hand, they are also ideal for use in a range of recipes, their unique flavour making them perfect for savoury as well as sweet applications. We'd particularly recommend capitalising on the velvety smooth flesh to make delicious smoothies, but they are also well-suited to baking scrumptious banana bread, adding some fruity goodness to your breakfast, and stirring into curries! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including a superb banana tiramisu, the ultimate dessert for fruit lovers!
As well as being delicious, kolikuttu bananas are extremely nutritious. Rich in potassium and fibre, and renowned for the rapid energy boost they provide eaters, they make the perfect healthy snack! We also sell frozen kolikuttu bananas! Fresh bananas have simply been peeled and then frozen, with no additives or preservatives added during the freezing process. As they're 100% pure, you can be confident that they are as healthy as the fresh fruits, and that they'll offer the same wonderful sweet-sour notes!

Name: Banana - matoke
Description:
Our matoke bananas from Uganda are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
These bananas are small to medium in size and are short and plump in shape. They are harvested when they are still green, before they have fully matured - these unripe bananas are perfect for cooking, particularly boiling, steaming, and roasting! Their dense, starchy flesh becomes significantly softer once cooked, and this tender flesh provides distinct sour notes, meaning it is ideal for combining into savoury meals. Indeed, the dish resulting from steam-cooked, mashed matoke bananas is considered a national staple in both Uganda and Rwanda!
Although they are most commonly utilised as green cooking bananas, if you leave the matoke bananas to ripen fully (with the skin becoming a vibrant yellow), you can also enjoy them as dessert bananas, simply eating fresh out of hand as you would with other banana varieties! Once fully mature, the bananas delight the tastebuds with their divine sweetness and subtly bitter aftertaste. The ripe bananas are ideal for use in any sweet or savoury recipe calling for bananas - from banana bread and ice cream to topping porridge and yoghurt, their astounding taste will shine through to make any dish or sweet treat a real delight. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including scrumptious mini banoffee pies!
As well as being delicious and versatile, matoke bananas are nutritionally beneficial. In particular, they are rich in dietary fibre and a good source of protein.

Name: Baobab pod
Description:
With a delicious taste and a 'superfood' status, our baobabs from Nigeria are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Although native to Africa, Australia, and Madagascar, baobabs have become globally renowned. These tough brown pods are medium to large in size - often roughly the size of a coconut - and round to oval in shape. Externally, they have firm, velvety shells and brown stems - the shells vary in toughness, some requiring a hammer or other tool to crack them open but others being able to be cracked by hand. Once opened, baobabs reveal many pieces of delicious, dry, cream-coloured pulp encasing hard seeds. The slightly chewy, sweet-sour pulp is either eaten fresh or dissolved in milk or water to make a delightfully refreshing drink, which many people say has a taste reminiscent of lemonade! The seeds can be eaten too and possess a rich, acidic taste somewhat similar to Brazil nuts. The pulp and the seeds are usually eaten separately, as the two have contrasting flavours that taste unpleasant when combined.
Baobabs are praised for their culinary versatility, being perfect for making a range of sweet and savoury food and drink recipes! Although most commonly mixed with milk and honey or sugar to make a sweet and refreshing drink, there are lots of regional variations in culinary use. For example, in Angola, the pulp is usually boiled and the resulting broth is used as the base for a type of ice cream known as gelado de múcua, and in Zimbabwe, the crushed crumbly pulp is stirred into porridge! The pulp can be ground in a powder too which is a perfect ingredient for sauces, jams, and baked goods such as cookies - if you don't want to make your own powder, why not buy some 100% pure baobab powder from our shop? Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including scrumptious baobab muffins!
As well as being delicious, baobabs stand out amongst other fruits in their nutritional value: they are rich in vitamin C, have 4 times the amount of potassium as bananas, and are a great source of calcium!

Just like our other My Exotic Fruit powders, our baobab powder is 100% pure so you can be comfortable in knowing that you're consuming only pure fruit. No nasty chemicals, preservatives, flavourings or sweeteners are added!
If you want to incorporate a new and exciting baobab product into your diet and benefit from its nutritional properties, then this powder is perfect for you. Conveniently packed in small packets you can either take this in your bag to use on the go, or you may prefer to purchase our bulk packs and enjoy it regularly at home.

Name: Bat nut - fresh and dried
Description:
Bat nuts are native to warm temperate parts of Eurasia and Africa where they have been cultivated for their edible seeds for at least 3,000 years. They grow on floating plants in slow-moving water up to 5m deep.
The ornately shaped fruits resemble the head of a bull or the silhouette of a flying bat. Their striking appearance looks man-made, and upon first glance, many people can't believe they are natural. Each fruit contains a large, starchy seed, which (once boiled) tastes similar to chestnut and firm potato. They're best eaten with a sprinkle of salt.
They're ready to harvest in the autumn and are only available for a short period of time.
In India and Pakistan, bat nuts are known as singhara or paniphal (eastern India) where they are widely cultivated in freshwater lakes. When the fruit has been dried, it's ground into a flour called singhare ka atta, which can be consumed as a phalahar (fruit diet) on the Hindu fasting days, the navratas. The flour is also used for making bread.
Not only are the bat nuts used as food, they are also a popular decorative item. In Southeast Asia, local people wash and polish them and then make various handicrafts including necklaces. Water caltrop are not eaten raw, they are boiled or roasted first.

Name: Batoko plum
Description:
Our batoko plums from Sri Lanka are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Despite their name, bakoto plums (also known as 'lovi-lovi') are not in fact a variety of plum but are rather small berries. These minuscule - they average between 1 and 2cm in diameter! - round to oval-shaped berries somewhat resemble cherries, boasting smooth, glossy, firm skin that catches the eye with its deep red hue. Beneath their taut skin is yellowish-white flesh that is crisp in texture and primarily sour in flavour, although providing subtle sweet notes too. The flesh contains an inedible seed that should be removed before eating.
Although they are edible when raw, batoko plums are not typically eaten fresh out of hand due to their bitter notes. Instead, they are usually utilised for making chutneys, jams, preserves, and syrups. They are also often stewed with sugar to turn these acidic fruits into a sweet dessert! The flesh can additionally be added to smoothies, combined into your morning granola or porridge, and incorporated into your favourite baked goods recipes, from pies and tarts to cobblers and cakes! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some wonderful recipes, including batoko plum jam and even batoko plum wine!
As well as being supremely versatile, batoko plums have been used for centuries in traditional Ayurvedic medicine, and are still today regarded as being nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are rich in dietary fibre and provide a good amount of calcium and potassium.

Name: Chilli - Bird's eye
Description:
Looking for a new way to add some spiciness to your mealtimes? Bird's eye chillies (also known as 'red Thai chillies') are just the thing for you: although minuscule in size, they pack a punch in flavour!
These chilli peppers historically originated from Mexico but today are most extensively cultivated and consumed in Thailand. They most likely got their unique name from their shape: small and rounded, they resemble a bird's eye! Their smooth, glossy exterior typically ripens from green to an eye-catching bright red. The mature red chillies are fruitier and sweeter than the more bitter, immature green peppers, and they boast a heat rating of 50,000-100,000 Scoville units, making them 10 to 20 times hotter than a jalapeno pepper, which averages around 5000 Scoville units!
Many people find them too hot to eat fresh out of hand. Instead, therefore, these staple ingredients in Thai cuisine tend to be used in small quantities in cooked applications, being ideal for bringing some vibrant colour and a kick of heat to soups, pastas, stir-fries, and curries! They are also perfect for making salsas and marinades, and for grinding into a spicy powder. Make sure to scoop out the small white seeds in the centre of each chilli if you want to reduce the heat intensity. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes, including one for making peri-peri sauce!
As well as being delicious and versatile, bird's eye chillies provide a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and they contain the chemical component capsaicin, which is believed to aid digestion.

Name: Bitter kola
Description:
Did you ever wonder how Coca-Cola got its name? Well, look no further than the bitter kola plant!
Also known as 'bitter cola' or 'Garcinia Kola', bitter kola originates from West and Central Africa, where it has been highly valued in traditional African herbal medicine for centuries! However, it may be more well known today as the original flavouring of Coca-Cola: some of the first recipes for the popular beverage included bitter kola extract!
Inside the orange-sized fruit is a yellow pulp, surrounding four seeds. Whilst they are sometimes eaten, the fruits of the bitter kola plant are extremely sour, so they are usually harvested for the seeds instead.
The seeds are chewed when raw. They have a bitter, wonderfully aromatic flavour, somewhat similar to that of a raw coffee bean with a sweet and peppery aftertaste! Once the pulp has no flavour remaining, you should spit it out.
You can also use the bitter kola to make a delightful tea - check out the 'Further information' tab below for a YouTube video demonstrating how to make this lovely beverage!
Bitter kola are however not consumed as a food source but rather for the multitude of health benefits which it brings. Among its impressive nutritional qualities, bitter kola is believed to be rich in calcium, vitamin C, and iron, and may be beneficial in treating inflammation and diabetes. It's advised to use no more than 2 bitter kola per day, which you should chew and then spit out. Take it after a meal, rather than on an empty stomach.

Name: Black corn
Description:
Calling all sweetcorn lovers: if you've never tried black corn, now is the time!
In appearance, black sweetcorn (also known as purple sweetcorn) looks the same as the corn on the cob we are all used to - black corn is botanically classified as 'zea mays', which is the same species as regular corn - except instead of bright yellow, the kernels are an eye-catching jet black in colour (some varieties have white kernels whilst they are immature, developing their black colour once they are fully ripe). Black corn grows in elongated cobs, typically reaching around 20cm in length, and is considered a medium-sized variety.
The kernels of black corn are chewy and starchy. Whilst black sweetcorn is not as sugary as modern varieties of yellow corn, it still delights the tastebuds with a subtle, yet wonderful, sweetness. Ideal for bringing some colour to your mealtimes, be aware that if you eat directly from the cob you will get some of the black oils on your fingers as they develop a sticky texture once cooked! However, the messiness is well worth the delicious flavour.
Black corn can be enjoyed in many different ways. It is well-suited to roasting, grilling, boiling and steaming - simply add a knob of butter and a sprinkle of salt and pepper to perfect the flavour! We recommend using black corn in any recipe that calls for yellow corn to add some variety to your diet. Why not grind the kernels into cornmeal and use it to make cornbread, tortillas, and Indian roti bread, or follow Peruvian tradition by boiling the corn to make the summer drink 'chicha morada'? Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including a light black corn salad, the perfect summer dish.
As well as boasting a striking colour that stuns the eyes and a delectable taste, black corn is also supremely nutritionally valuable. It is rich in anthocyanins, a plant pigment that has numerous anti-inflammatory and antioxidant benefits, and also contains important minerals and nutrients such as iron, magnesium, vitamin A, folate, and phosphorus.

Calling all sweetcorn lovers: if you've never tried black corn, now is the time!
In appearance, black sweetcorn (also known as purple sweetcorn) looks the same as the corn on the cob we are all used to - black corn is botanically classified as 'zea mays', which is the same species as regular corn - except instead of bright yellow, the kernels are an eye-catching jet black in colour (some varieties have white kernels whilst they are immature, developing their black colour once they are fully ripe). Black corn grows in elongated cobs, typically reaching around 20cm in length, and is considered a medium-sized variety.
The kernels of black corn are chewy and starchy. Whilst black sweetcorn is not as sugary as modern varieties of yellow corn, it still delights the tastebuds with a subtle, yet wonderful, sweetness. Ideal for bringing some colour to your mealtimes, be aware that if you eat directly from the cob you will get some of the black oils on your fingers as they develop a sticky texture once cooked! However, the messiness is well worth the delicious flavour.
Black corn can be enjoyed in many different ways. It is well-suited to roasting, grilling, boiling and steaming - simply add a knob of butter and a sprinkle of salt and pepper to perfect the flavour! We recommend using black corn in any recipe that calls for yellow corn to add some variety to your diet. Why not grind the kernels into cornmeal and use it to make cornbread, tortillas, and Indian roti bread, or follow Peruvian tradition by boiling the corn to make the summer drink 'chicha morada'? Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including a light black corn salad, the perfect summer dish.
As well as boasting a striking colour that stuns the eyes and a delectable taste, black corn is also supremely nutritionally valuable. It is rich in anthocyanins, a plant pigment that has numerous anti-inflammatory and antioxidant benefits, and also contains important minerals and nutrients such as iron, magnesium, vitamin A, folate, and phosphorus.

Name: Black sapote 'chocolate pudding fruit'
Description:
For us here in the UK, the black sapote represents the holy grail of fruits. It's no wonder then that it is a clear customer favourite and is one of the most sought-after fruits in the country!
Black sapote are a small to medium-sized fruit which are native to Mexico, Central America, and Colombia, but are now also cultivated in the USA and the Philippines (due to its sensitive nature, it isn't grown commercially on a significant scale, nor is it exported around the world in large quantities). Their shape somewhat resembles Bramley cooking apples and they can be a similar size too. The skin of the fruit is bright green turning to olive green as they mature on the tree, and finally shifts to very dark green to brown once they are ripe and ready to eat. It can be hard to recognise the slight colour change of mature fruits from bright green to olive green. Experienced pickers are needed to ensure only the mature fruits are harvested. In order to reduce disruption to the tree and avoid ripe fruits being knocked and falling to the floor, a long harvest pole with a fabric net is used to cut and pick the fruit.
The glossy dark brown flesh of the fruit is soft, loose and buttery. It's like a really soft, slightly-mashed avocado. There are usually a few medium-sized seeds in the middle of the fruit.
Wondering what the reason is for the excitement surrounding black sapote? A hint lies in its nickname, 'chocolate pudding fruit' - as a nation of chocolate lovers, we're instantly attracted to anything with chocolate in its name! The ripe flesh of black sapote certainly does look like chocolate mousse and has virtually the same texture too. Whilst the flavour is not the same as chocolate mousse, some people do note subtle chocolate-like flavours amongst other wonderful flavours including honey, date and caramel. This heavenly combination makes for a real treat for the tastebuds! We would regard this fruit as medium-sweet to sweet with a subtle delicate flavour.
As well as being delicious, black sapote also boast a number of health benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C, providing more than 6 times the daily requirement! Additionally, they contain good amounts of calcium and phosphorous.

Tab Content:Also Known As:
Chocolate pudding fruit, zapote prieto, sapote, sapote negro, zapote, zapote negro, zapote de mico, matasano (or matazano) de mico, ebano, black persimmon (in Hawaii).

Diospyros nigra.
Tab Content:Origin: Our black sapote is sourced from various regions in the tropics.
Tab Content:Preparation:
Always wash before eating.

Black sapote should be left to ripen at room temperature. They are ready to eat when very soft all over. You may also notice the skin starting to shrivel or wrinkle. It must be completely soft to touch to be ready to eat.

Unripe fruits which have a bright-green colour take around 14 days from harvest to ripen. 

Fruits which are riper, have an olive-green exterior and will ripen in 2 to 6 days from harvest.

Once the black sapote arrive at your address you will usually need to ripen them for up to 3 weeks before they are ready to eat. In the smmer months the fruits ripen quicker however in the winter it can take weeks for them to ripen fully.

Our frozen black sapote pulp is ready to eat.
Tab Content:Usage:
The best way to enjoy a black sapote is to simply eat it fresh, straight out of hand. Enjoy the delicate, soft, delicious flesh just as it is.

The black sapote is also suitable for use in drink and dessert applications. It's perfect for making ice cream or being used as a pie/pastry filling

-

See below for some interesting ways in which the black sapote is used across the world:

Philippines - the ripe flesh is served as dessert with a little milk poured over it. This dessert is also sometimes made with orange juice instead of milk.

Mexico - the flesh is made into a smooth pulp and mixed with orange juice or brandy. It's served with cream. Another variation is to mix the pulp with wine, cinnamon and sugar.

USA, Florida -  the flesh is blended into a smooth pulp with milk and nutmeg. Drinks enthusiasts might like to try blending the flesh with pineapple juice.

Central America - the fruits are fermented and made into a liqueur which is similar to brandy.
Tab Content:Storage:
Wrap fresh black sapote in tissue paper and leave in a warm place to ripen.

Once soft, they can be kept in refrigeration for a few days.

Though black sapote will remain fit for eating if held for a few days in refrigeration, they will be too soft to stand handling.

Frozen black sapote should be refrigerated and consumed within 2 days or you can refreeze immediately and use by the best before date shown on the packet.
Tab Content:Average Weight: The average weight of the black sapote we source is between 320g to 450g per fruit. However, please note that there are natural variations in fresh fruit.
Tab Content:Further Info:
An article about black sapote on www.theguardian.com written by Palisa Anderson on 09/10/20.

The wood of the back sapote tree is yellowish with unusual markings near the heart of older specimens. It's suitable for cabinetwork but underused.

The crushed bark and leaves are applied to blisters in the Philippines.

Name: Blue olive
Description:
Our blue olives from Sri Lanka are a must-try!

Name: Breadfruit - breadfruit seeds (ukwa)
Description:
Beneath the breadfruit seed shell you will find the breadfruit nut, this is a healthy alternative to other carby foods such as crisps.
Commonly eaten in East Africa, although now this delicacy has spread across the globe to other cultures and origins. Breadfruit, often referred to as a 'tropical potato' is related to mulberry, fig and jackfruit.
It grows easily in many regions across the tropics, requires minimal care and bares fruit quickly - up to 200kg per year. Breadfruit trees are also drought resistant and can survive tropical storms. It is for this reason that is a staple part of the diet of millions of people.
Ripe breadfruit has creamy to yellow flesh, with a custard-like texture and is sweet to taste, similar to jackfruit, corn and durian.
Cooked breadfruit has a bread-like texture and aroma with a flavour that is between potato, artichoke and chestnut.
Breadfruit is high in carbohydrates and a good source of antioxidants, calcium, carotenoids, dietary fiber, energy, iron, magnesium, omega 3 and omega 6, to name just a few.

Name: Burmese grape
Description:
Burmese grapes are small round fruits with a cream coloured peel which is removed before eating. Some fruits taste sweet whilst others are brightly sour and some are even sweet and sour.
The Burmese grapes are somewhat similar to long kong, a fruit commonly found in Southeast Asia.
Apart from their sweet-sour taste, Burmese grape is a good source of nutrients, vitamins and minerals. Consuming 100 grams of Burmese grapes offers 55mg of vitamin C, 3.3mg of iron, 10.5g of carbohydrate, 0.7g of protein, 0.3g of total fat and 2mg of Calcium.

Name: Cacao fruit, frozen pulp
Description:
Our frozen cacao fruit pulp has a sweet and tart tropical flavour suitable for many fruit blends.The tropical flavour of cacao fruit pulp has been likened to soursop and mangosteen (both delicious fruits) and also 'passionfruit lemonade'...imagine a tangy and refreshing lemonade made with fresh passionfruit pulp!
The most popular use of this frozen pulp is juice making, or in cocktails but don't forget sorbet and ice creams! Drinks made from cacao beans and/or pulp are the drink of choice for both nourishing and medicinal qualities.
The use of the cacao fruit dates back around 2000 years. The Aztecs called it 'the food of the gods'. It's native to the Amazon and is still used in the region today as a staple part of their diet.
The pulp is believed to hold multiple nutritional benefits includng powerful antioxidants as well as being delicious and unique. Give it a try, we're sure you'll like it! We have cacao fruit pulp with and without the cacao beans.
The pulp without the cacao beans is processed and frozen in Brazil, it's made from the sweet white pulp of the cacao fruit, rather than the bitter dark beans that are used to make chocolate.
The pulp with cacao beans is processed and frozen here in the UK.

Name: Carob bean - nature's chocolate
Description:
The carob tree is a species of flowering evergreen tree in the pea family, fabaceae.
It's cultivated for its edible pods. Carob is mildly sweet and is used in powdered, chip, or syrup form as an ingredient in cakes and cookies, and as a substitute for cocoa powder.
Carob consumed by humans is the dried (and sometimes roasted) pod. The pod consists of two main parts: the pulp accounts for 90% and the seeds for 10% of the pod weight.
A traditional sweet, eaten during Lent and Good Friday, is also made from carob pods in Malta. Dried carob fruit is traditionally eaten on the Jewish holiday of Tu Bishvat.
In Cyprus, carob syrup is known as Cyprus's black gold, and is widely exported. In Malta, a syrup (ulepp tal-arrub) is made out of carob pods. This is a traditional medicine for coughs and sore throat. Carob syrup is also used in Crete as a natural sweetener, and is considered a natural source of calcium.
Carob juice drinks are traditionally drunk during the Islamic month of Ramadan.
Carob bars, an alternative to chocolate bars, are often available in health-food stores.
Due to its strong pleasant taste, it can be found mixed with orange or chocolate.
In Libya, carob syrup (called rub) is used as a complement to Asida (Asida is a dish made up of a cooked wheat flour lump of dough, sometimes with added butter or honey. Similar to gruel or porridge, it is eaten in many North African countries.)
Carob contains three times more calcium than milk. It is also rich in iron, phosphorus, and dietary fibre.

Name: Carrot - purple
Description:
Looking for a way to add some colour to your diet? Our purple carrots are just the thing for you!
Purple carrots resemble standard supermarket-bought carrots in size and shape. However, they immediately catch the eye with their distinctive deep purple hue! Yet, although their thin, delicate outer skin is purple, they actually retain an orange centre, which gives them a most unique appearance indeed! They wow with their flavour too: they boast a subtly peppery flavour, with distinct notes of sweetness.
These gently spicy carrots are most commonly eaten raw, as this is thought to be the best way to maximise their nutritional benefits. However, they can also be used in any way you'd utilise orange carrots: from steaming and mashing to roasting and juicing, these carrots will be brilliant, vibrant additions to your mealtimes! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including dazzling purple carrot hummus!
Not only do purple carrots stand out in their colour, but they stand out in their health benefits too! This is because, like purple potatoes, they get their attractive purple colour from anthocyanin, a powerful antioxidant which is believed to boost the immune system. They also contain 20% less sugar than the standard orange variety, making them perfect for those on a low-sugar diet. Additionally, purple carrots contain vitamins B, C and E and are a good source of dietary fibre.

Name: Cashew apple (with cashew nut attached) - frozen
Description:
The cashew apple is the fleshy part of the cashew fruit attached to the cashew nut. Cashew nuts are well known and more widely traded than the cashew fruits, because the fruits are easily bruised and have a short shelf life.
The top end of the cashew apple is attached to the stem that comes off the tree. The bottom end of the cashew apple attaches to the cashew nut, which is encased in a shell. In botanical terms, the cashew apple is an accessory fruit that grows on the cashew seed (which is the nut).
The cashew apple can have an astringent taste which is sometimes removed by steaming the fruit for five minutes before washing it in cold water.
Cashew apple juice is delicious and has a lot of potential to become a mainstream drink of the future.

Tab Content:Preparation:
After defrosting the cashew apples are ready to eat. The shell with the cashew nut must not be eaten.

Wash before eating.

CAUTION: The cashew shell attached to the fruit contains oil compounds that can cause contact dermatitis if handled incorrectly.

Use gloves when removing the shell and take care not to break it.
Tab Content:Usage:
The cashew apple can be eaten fresh, cooked in curries, or fermented into vinegar, as well as an alcoholic drink.

It is also used to make preserves, chutneys, and jams in some countries such as India and Brazil.

In many countries, particularly in South America, the cashew apple is used to make juice and flavour alcoholic drinks including cocktails.

In Goa, the cashew apple is mashed and the juice extracted and kept for fermentation for a few days. Fermented juice then undergoes a double distillation process. The resulting beverage is called feni or fenny. Feni is about 40–42% alcohol. The single-distilled version is called urrac, which is about 15% alcohol.

In Tanzania, the cashew apple is used to make a strong liqueur named gongo and in Mozambique, cashew farmers commonly make a strong liqueur from the fruits after they have been left to lose water and ferment. The shrivelled fruits are used for distillation.
Tab Content:Storage: Keep in the refrigerator and use within a day or two or refreeze immediately upon arrival.

Cempedak is a sought after fruit from Southeast Asia which is regarded as one of the most delicious fruits in the world by some fruit hunters!
The flavour and aroma of cempedak is like a combination of breadfruit, jackfruit and a hint of durian. It's described as sweeter than honey.

Name: Ceylon olive
Description:
Our Ceylon olives from Sri Lanka are a must-try!
Ceylon olives immediately catch the eye with their nearly perfectly spherical shape and smooth, glossy, green skin. Beneath the appealing skin of these small fruits - they measure only 2.5cm in length! - is firm green flesh that is somewhat reminiscent of avocado in texture. Once fully ripe, this pasty flesh boasts a delicious savour: they have a tangy, sour taste which some say is comparable to that of Meditteranean olives.
Being pleasingly bite-sized, Ceylon olives are perfect for eating fresh out of hand. However, they are also extremely versatile - they are well-suited for both sweet and savoury applications! In their native Sri Lanka, they are popular ingredients in a variety of recipes: they are boiled and combined with cooked dishes; used to make delectable chutneys and pickles, and often sprinkled in chilli flakes and salt to create mouthwatering snacks! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including an olive and ambarella accharu (achcharu), a wonderful Sri Lankan pickle dish!
As well as boasting an appetizing taste and culinary versatility, Ceylon olives have also been used in traditional Sri Lankan medicine for centuries, and today they are still highly regarded for their nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and provide a good amount of vitamin C.

Ceylon olives immediately catch the eye with their nearly perfectly spherical shape and smooth, glossy, green skin. As well as boasting an appetizing taste and culinary versatility, Ceylon olives have also been used in traditional Sri Lankan medicine for centuries, and today they are still highly regarded for their nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and provide a good amount of vitamin C.

Name: Chui jhal
Description:
Looking for a way to spice up your diet? Chui jhal is just the thing!
Chui, also known as 'piper chaba' and 'piper chilli', is a plant native to south and southeast Asia. It is especially valued as a culinary herb in India and Bangladesh. In Bangladesh, it is called 'chui jhal', and is most widely found in the Jashore, Khulna, Satkhira and Bagerhat districts of the country. Chui jhal is one of the most popular spices in southern Bangladesh, and the chopped stems, roots, and skin of the plant are all utilised in cooking and traditional medicine. Indeed, it is one of the most expensive spices you can buy there!
We sell the roots of the plant. They are elongated and thick, with rough brown skin. They have an intense aroma which fills the room, and a strong, spicy taste that makes them ideal for use as a flavouring - they are said to have a taste somewhat reminiscent of horseradish! Perfect for adding some much-needed heat to any number of savoury dishes, in Bangladesh, it is common to incorporate chopped chui jhal roots with meat and fish dishes, especially with mutton and beef curries, to enhance their flavour. Try adding small, chopped pieces 10-15 minutes before the curry is cooked! In Thailand, chui jhal is known as 'dee plee' and is consumed in both fresh and dried forms. It is often ground using a mortar and pestle, and this powder features as an ingredient in a variety of Thai sauces and pastes, as well as soups. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration!
As well as being ideal for bringing a kick of flavour to your mealtimes, chui jhal has been a staple of Ayurvedic medicine for centuries, and is still today believed to boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, it is thought to have anti-inflammatory properties and beneficial phytochemicals. Infusing chui jhal and ginger in boiling water and drinking the resulting soothing herbal tea is believed to help alleviate colds.

Name: Citrus - bergamot
Description:
Citrus bergamia, more commonly known as bergamot orange, are wonderful fruits!
A fragrant citrus fruit the size of an orange, bergamots are hybrid fruits that derive their name from the Italian city of Bergamo. Bergamots have glossy, smooth skin that is delightfully aromatic and shifts from green to bright yellow as the fruit ripens.
Indeed, if you're looking for a photogenic fruit, we'd recommend our leafy bergamots! These bergamots have been cut from the tree with their leaves (as well as a little bit of the branch) still attached. The heightened natural element of these bergamots makes their appearance supremely attractive, so they are ideal for fruit photography. (Please note that the leaves and stems may detatch in transit. If you require bergamot with leaves and stems still attached, please email us at info@myexoticfruit.com before ordering)
Beneath the rind is soft, pale, sour yellow flesh that is divided into approximately 10 segments and is intensely fragrant and juicy. However, although the flesh of the bergamot is edible, the fruits are most often used for the juice extracted from the flesh. The juice has an acidic, tart taste comparable to other citrus fruits, but is notably less sour than lemon (although they are more bitter than grapefruit).
The juice is most commonly used to add a kick of citrus flavour to a variety of food and drink recipes. The rind and zest are often used to make syrups, cocktails and jams, with its use in marmalade-making being particularly pronounced in Italy. Bergamots work well with other citrus fruits, and pair successfully with seafood, ricotta, avocado, and fresh herbs. For those with a sweet tooth, bergamot is ideal for bringing a touch of exotic flavour to your favourite recipes for baked goods such as cookies and cakes - check out the 'Further information' tab below for a mouthwatering recipe for a bergamot and rosemary cookies! In Bergamo, the oil extracted from the rind is used in perfumes, colognes, teas, and confectionaries - the essence is used to flavour a variety of items, from Earl Grey tea to Turkish delight!
In Sweden and Norway, Bergamot is a very common flavourant in snus, a smokeless tobacco product. Likewise, in dry nasal snuff, it is also a common aroma in traditional blends.
As well as being extremely versatile in their culinary uses, bergamot boasts a range of nutritional benefits: they are an excellent source of vitamin C and potassium, and are rich in vitamins B1, B2 and A.


Our bergamot will generally be green at the start of the season but by end of the season they will be yellow. If the colour is important, please check with us before ordering by emailing info@myexoticfruit.com.

Name: Citrus - bergamot, dried
Description:
Citrus bergamia, more commonly known as bergamot oranges, are wonderful fruits!
A fragrant citrus fruit the size of an orange, bergamots are hybrid fruits that derive their name from the Italian city of Bergamo. Bergamots have glossy, smooth skin that is delightfully aromatic and shifts from green to bright yellow as the fruit ripens - bergamot differs from other citrus fruits in that its peel is edible!
Beneath the rind is soft, pale, sour yellow flesh that is divided into approximately 10 segments and is intensely fragrant and juicy. However, although the flesh of the bergamot is edible, the fruits are most often used for the juice extracted from the flesh. The juice has an acidic, tart taste comparable to other citrus fruits, but is notably less sour than lemon (although they are more bitter than grapefruit).
Delightfully aromatic - an essence extracted from the fragrant skin of this sour fruit is used to flavour Earl Grey and Lady Grey teas, as well as confectionery, including Turkish delight! - the flavour of bergamot flesh is compared to a delicious combination of sour orange and lemon, with a powerful citrus taste and intense sour kick.
Like the fresh fruit, our dried bergamot peel (sold in 50g and 500g packets) is a superior culinary ingredient. Hailing from Calabria (where 90% of the world's bergamots are grown!), the peels are dried in the Italian sunshine and will work well in any number of recipes, from making distinctive jams, marmalades, and preserves, to imparting divine citrus notes to soups, rice, and stir-fries. Intensely aromatic and jam-packed with essential oils, the peels are perfect for bringing a distinct kick of flavour to your favourite sweet and savoury recipes!
Indeed, the peels are particularly well suited to making a variety of alcoholic drinks and for that reason have become favoured by gin distillers. They can also be used in baking - we'd recommend adding some dried bergamot peel to muffin and cake batter, as well as your favoured bread dough! Using dried bergamot peel means you can avoid the laborious task of peeling fruits, so you can create your scrumptious baked goods even quicker!

Description:
Once you've tried our speciality Ippolito oranges, you'll never return to regular supermarket-bought oranges! They're only in season for a short period each year, so buy them while you can!
Ippolito oranges, cultivated in Spain and Italy, are widely considered some of the most delicious oranges that can be found anywhere in the world. A variety of blood orange, they have soft, visually attractive bright orange and deep red peel and dazzling red flesh that is incredibly juicy and sweet. Not as tangy or with such an intense citrus flavour as other blood oranges, they are ideal for those who prefer sweeter fruits than the usual tartness and sharpness of citrus fruits.
Delectable when eaten fresh out of hand, Ippolito oranges are also ideal for a number of culinary uses. They are commonly used to create marmalade, orange juice with a stunning red hue, and to add a touch of intense fruity flavour to baked goods by adding in some zest. Indeed, they work perfectly in all recipes calling for blood oranges. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes, including one for an incredible chocolate and orange torte!
As well as having a mouthwatering taste, Ippolito oranges additionally boast a range of nutritional benefits. They are a particularly excellent source of vitamin C and are also rich in dietary fibre and many antioxidants.

Name: Citrus - blood orange 'sanguinelli'
Description:
Why have supermarket-bought oranges when incredibly eye-catching sanguinelli blood oranges exist?
The blood orange is a natural mutation of the orange. Medium to large in size, round in shape, and with orange rind (which sometimes has a light red blush), from the outside these Spanish blood oranges look like typical oranges. However, once you peel back their smooth skin, you are greeted with astounding orange to deep burgundy flesh - the sanguinelli variety is usually a lighter red in colour than other varieties and slightly more sporadic in colouring - that delights the sight!
The beautiful, soft flesh emits a wonderfully fragrant aroma, and your tastebuds will be wowed after only one bite: like all blood oranges, sanguinelli are intensely juicy, supremely refreshing, slightly tangy, and less acidic than regular oranges. Bright, floral notes and undertones of raspberry and cherry make these sweet-sour fruits a brilliant taste sensation!
Blood oranges are usually eaten fresh out of hand. However, these fruits are also very well suited to a number of culinary applications. Indeed, they are a popular choice among chefs and bartenders! Across Europe, sanguinelli rind is used in biscotti, to flavour desserts, pastries, and creams, and it is served with olives and red onions and tossed into salads. We'd recommend using them to create a scrumptious marmalade to add a citrus kick to your toast; make invigorating juice, perfect for drinking by itself or adding to cocktails, syrups and marinades; add the zest into your favourite baking recipes, from cakes to biscuits, or why not follow the Spaniards by serving it over Serrano ham, garlic, and grilled bread as a breakfast dish? The opportunities are endless! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including a recipe for blood orange donuts, the perfect fruity treat!
As well as being mouthwatering, blood oranges also boast a number of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and dietary fibre - a medium-sized blood orange provides 28% of the recommended daily intake of dietary fibre! - and their red pigment anthocyanin is an antioxidant, meaning blood oranges contain much greater amounts of antioxidants than other oranges.

The sweet-sour taste, with bright, floral notes and undertones reminiscent of raspberries and cherries makes for a brilliant taste sensation.
Although often eaten fresh out of hand, moro are very well suited to a number of culinary applications. Indeed, blood oranges are a popular choice among chefs and bartenders! We'd recommend using them to create a scrumptious marmalade to add a citrus kick to your toast; make invigorating juice, perfect for drinking by itself or adding to cocktails, syrups and marinades; add the zest into your favourite baking recipes, from cakes to biscuits, or why not make the popular Sicilian winter salad by combining sliced Blood oranges, sliced bulb fennel, and olive oil? The opportunities are endless! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including a recipe for blood orange donuts, the perfect fruity treat!

In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and dietary fibre - a medium-sized blood orange provides 28% of the recommended daily intake of dietary fibre! - and their red pigment anthocyanin is an antioxidant, meaning blood oranges contain much greater amounts of antioxidants than other oranges.

Name: Citrus - buddha's hand
Description:
Looking for a unique exotic fruit to try? Buddha's hand is just the thing for you!
Buddha's hand, cultivated in Asia for thousands of years, is an unusually shaped citron variety - its fruit is segmented into long finger-like sections, together almost resembling a human hand! The different cultivars and variations of this citron variety form a gradient from "open-hand" types, with outward-splayed segments, to "closed-hand" types, in which the fingers are kept together.
The bumpy, bright yellow (when fully mature) rind is covered with small oil glands that release a divine aroma with notes of lavender and lemon. Unlike other citrus fruits, most varieties of the Buddha's hand fruit contain no pulp, seeds, or juice. Instead, beneath the fragrant, bitter-sweet peel is dense, spongy, white pith with a floral, sweet flavour that will delight your tastebuds.
The peel and pith are primarily used as zest to add tropical flavour to a range of dishes - given its bitter-sweet taste range, it works well in both sweet and savoury recipes! Indeed, we'd recommend using it as an exotic substitute for lemon zest in any recipe calling for a kick of citrus goodness. As well as zesting, the pith and peel can be cut into slices and then used to infuse liquors, olive oils, sugars, and salts. Chopped pith can also be candied to become a sweet chewy treat, turned into mouthwatering marmalades and syrups, or used to flavour tea. If you're looking for a way to really impress people, why not follow Chinese tradition - in China, the Buddhas hand citron symbolises happiness and long life - and cut the pith of Buddha's hand into decorative shapes to (once candied) display as edible centrepieces for dinner parties? Indeed, in Japan, it is a favourite gift for New Year's as it is believed to bestow good fortune on a household! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including Buddha's hand shortbread and a yoghurt and Buddha's hand cake!
As well as being culinarily versatile, Buddhas hand boasts a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, it is a fantastic source of vitamin C and contains dietary fibre (which aids digestion), calcium, and vitamin E.

Tab Content:Preparation: Ripe and ready to use. Wash first.
Tab Content:Usage: Though renowned for its exquisite form and aroma, the Buddha’s hand fruit can also be eaten (often as a zest or flavouring) in desserts, savoury dishes and alcoholic beverages (such as vodka) or candied as a sweet. The sliced, dried peel of immature fruits is also prescribed as a tonic in traditional medicine. Believe it or not, it's also used as a natural air freshener in South East Asian countries.
Tab Content:Storage:
Fresh: keep refrigerated and use within 1 to 2 weeks. Buddha's hand can also be frozen for future use.

Frozen: refrigerate when you receive it and use within 3–5 days. You may also refreeze it immediately upon arrival.
Tab Content:Average Weight: One Buddha's hand usually weighs approximately 400-600g. However, please note that there are natural variations in fresh fruit.
Tab Content:Further Info:
Wondering how best to enjoy your Buddha's hand citron? We'd recommend using it to make this amazing shortbread, a unique treat for all the family; this candied Buddha's hand for the ideal sweet, chewy snack, and this kale and fuyu persimmon salad, complemented by a wonderful Buddha's hand vinaigrette! 

We'd also recommend making a yoghurt and Buddha's hand cake - the recipe is below!

Ingredients

  • 1 Buddha's hand
  • 230g flour
  • 230g sugar
  • 125g yoghurt
  • 130ml sunflower/vegetable oil
  • 8g yeast
  • 3 eggs

Method

  1. Preheat the oven to 180°C and prepare a round cake tin.
  2. Mix the eggs and sugar.
  3. Add grated Buddha's hand, the yoghurt and the oil. Beat until they are perfectly combined.
  4. Incorporate the sifted flour with the yeast little by little.
  5. Pour the mixture into the tin and bake for about an hour.

Name: Citrus - buddha's hand, dried
Description:
Buddha's hand is close to one of the original citrus varieties, the citron, from which all citrus fruits are derived. However, they look nothing like typical citrus fruits - indeed, they are one of the most visually distinctive fruits we think you'll ever see!
An unusually shaped citrus, the fruit is segmented into finger-like sections, resembling a human hand, earning it its nickname. However, the different cultivars and variations of this citron variety form a gradient from "open-hand" types, with outward-splayed segments, to "closed-hand" types, in which the fingers are kept together. Its distinctive look has earned it much popularity throughout Asia: in China, the Buddhas hand citron symbolises happiness and long life and is often used in displays at home and temple altars, whilst in Japan, it is a favourite gift to celebrate the new year, as it is believed to bestow good fortune on a household.
Unlike other citrus fruits, most varieties of the Buddha's hand fruit contain no pulp or juice. Instead, they are entirely pith and rind. However, like the typical citrus fruits, Buddha's hand are extremely aromatic, offering a delightful fragrance comparable to a unique combination of lemon, vanilla, and dried walnut. They are so renowned for their bright, floral scent that in Asia it is common for people to use them to perfume their homes!
The dried slices of Buddha's hand, made up of the fruit's peel and pith, have been hand-prepared and sun-dried in the Mekong Delta of Vietnam, and offer the same wonderful aroma and perfumed bitterness. These dried slices are ideal for making drinks: simply infuse them with hot or cold water and you will instantly have a delectable drink! However, they are particularly favoured by gin distillers, and are exceedingly popular as an ingredient used to create a number of other alcoholic drinks, including vermouths, and vodkas. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for a recipe for an amazing Buddha's hand cocktail! They are also perfect for decorating drinks, especially for garnishing cocktails.

However, like the typical citrus fruits, Buddha's hand are extremely aromatic, offering a delightful fragrance comparable to a unique combination of lemon, vanilla, and dried walnut. They are so renowned for their bright, floral scent that in Asia it is common for people to use them to perfume their homes!
The dried slices of Buddha's hand, made up of the fruit's peel and pith, have been hand-prepared and sun-dried in the Mekong Delta of Vietnam, and offer the same wonderful aroma and perfumed bitterness. These dried slices are ideal for making drinks: simply infuse them with hot or cold water and you will instantly have a delectable drink! However, they are particularly favoured by gin distillers, and are exceedingly popular as an ingredient used to create a number of other alcoholic drinks, including vermouths, and vodkas. Name: Citrus - citron 'cedro lemon'
Description:
Citron are the ultimate citrus fruit!
They (known in its native Italy as 'cedro') are possibly the first citrus cultivated in Europe, possibly arriving from Persia, and have been cultivated for thousands of years in civilizations around the globe as a culinary ingredient, medicinal remedy, and religious symbol. They are one of the four 'original' citrus fruits, meaning that all other citrus varieties that are in existence today originate from citron.
We source our citron from Italy and Sri Lanka. The Sri Lanken citron has more of a perfumed aroma, whereas the Italian citron has a more of a conventional citrusy tangy aroma.
Citron are one of the largest varieties of citrus, measuring up to three times the size of a supermarket lemon. These immensely aromatic fruits have wrinkled skin that ripens from green to bright yellow, and is enveloped in prominent oil glands, giving the surface a pebbled, glossy appearance. Beneath the skin is a layer of thick, white pith (which constitutes approximately 70% of the entire fruit), encasing a small amount of flesh.
Unlike other citrus fruits, citron has very little juice and flesh, so are most commonly used for their spongy pith and oil-infused zest. The pith is surprisingly sweet and is commonly sliced into small pieces and tossed with sugar and herbs to add some bright citrus notes to salads or combined with balsamic vinaigrette to create a lively salad dressing. The rind has a flavour and fragrance reminiscent of lemons, and In Italy, the peel is customarily candied and enjoyed as a sweet delicacy. The juice of the citron fruit is used as a drink and often as a syrup too. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including a citron risotto!
As well as being versatile and divinely perfumed, citron boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre, potassium, and magnesium, and also provide good amounts of vitamin C, iron, and vitamin B6.

Name: Citrus - clementine
Description:
Looking for a new variety of citrus to try? Our Spanish leafy clementines are just the thing for you!
Once you peel back the glossy, textured, orange rind of these small to medium-sized fruits (usually 6-7cm in diameter), you will understand part of the reason why they're so highly praised - the way the flesh greets you with a glorious citrus fragrance that fills the room.
However, their flavour is just as divine. The segmented flesh is sublimely juicy and tender, with an intense aromatic taste and powerful notes of acidity that will wow your tastebuds. Wonderfully refreshing, succulent, and flavourful, they are also favoured because they usually contain no seeds (or a few at most), making them easier to eat.
Clementines make the perfect healthy snack, however their uniquely sweet and tart flavour profile also means they are ideal for a range of culinary applications. We'd recommend using them to add a citrus kick to cocktails and mocktails, create scrumptious fruity desserts and baked goods, and complement the sour, earthy notes in curries and meat dishes. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including a clementine, pistachio and cranberry meringue wreath and clementine martini!
Like other clementines, clementines boast a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and other antioxidants, and are rich in potassium and vitamin B6.

Name: Citrus - dekopon
Description:
Meet our newest citrus: Dekopon, also known as Sumo Citrus, with its unique appearance featuring a protruding neck and vibrant orange skin.
This fruit is exceptionally sweet, low in acidity, and bursting with juicy seedless segments. It has a thick rind that is easy to peel, revealing a fragrant aroma when peeled.
Dekopon are a Japanese hybrid citrus variety developed in the late 20th century, they were initially overlooked for their bumpy appearance but became prized for their exceptional sweetness.
These citrus fruits are perfect for eating fresh out of hand. Dekopons pair well with yogurt and make a great fresh topping for pancakes. You can also use them in salads or use their juice in marinades and dressings. We'd recommend using them to make desserts like tarts, muffins and cheesecakes.
As well as being versatile, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and A, calcium and iron.

Name: Citrus - etrog
Description:
Etrogs are must-try citrus delicacies!
They are a member of the citron family. They have been cultivated for thousands of years but are today one of the rarest citrus fruits around, being grown primarily for traditional Jewish rituals.
Whilst they look somewhat like an oblong lemon, etrogs are considerably larger than their more famous citrus counterpart, averaging 10-15cm in length! They dazzle the eye with both their shape, which can be compared to that of the flame of a candle, and their bright yellow skin.
The glossy yellow rind is thick, bumpy, and immensely fragrant, with a distinctive aroma of lemon and violets. Beneath the rind is spongy white pith that is sweet, yet with slightly bitter undertones. Like other citron varieties, the pith constitutes most of the fruit - etrogs only contain a little bit of pale yellow pulp. This seeded pulp is acidic, but not very juicy.
Etrog's aromatic rind and pith have made them a popular flavouring ingredient by people around the world! The pith and rind are boiled and then simmered in sugar to enhance their sweetness. The cooked etrog is perfect for incorporating into cakes, cookies, and other baked goods, and can also be candied as a sweet treat. We'd particularly recommend simmering etrog into marmalades, jellies, and jams and infusing it into vodka to impart a citrus, floral flavour.
Once defrosted, our frozen etrog can be used in the exact same way as our fresh etrog! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including etrog liquor!
As well as being versatile, etrog are nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are extremely rich in vitamin C and provide a good amount of dietary fibre and potassium. As our frozen etrog is made of 100% fruit, with no flavourings or colourings added, you can be confident in knowing that it is just as healthy as the fresh fruit!

Name: Citrus - flying dragon orange
Description:
Flying dragon oranges are citrus delicacies that all exotic fruit lovers need to try!
These delicious oranges gained their name from the twisted branches and long thorns of their trees which, when they are bare in the winter, resemble clawed dragons in mid-flight! Due to this eye-catching appearance, the fruit trees are highly regarded as an ornamental variety for private and public gardens, once being planted in the gardens of St Paul's Cathedral!
Flying dragons are native to China and Korea, however they are today cultivated around the world. They are small in size - typically measuring only 3-4cm in diameter! - and round in shape. They have a pebbled, orange rind that has a slightly velvety feel due to their downy coating. Beneath their textured skin is thin, white, spongy pith, attached to tender, yellow flesh that emits a glorious citrus fragrance and is sure to wow your tastebuds: the soft, seeded flesh is exceptionally juicy and intensely tart, astounding eaters with its combination of lemon-like tanginess and bitter notes of grapefruit. These acidic fruits have therefore earned the name 'bitter oranges'!
Like other citrus fruits, flying dragon oranges are not typically eaten fresh out of hand due to their sharp savour and little flesh content. Instead, they are primarily cooked to make delectable marmalades, syrups, jams, and jellies, and are often candied with sugar to create scrumptious chewy snacks! The peels can also be zested like lemons and limes to flavour everything from cakes to cocktails, garnish cocktails (and mocktails!), and create perfect seasoning powder by drying and grinding. A small amount of juice can be extracted from the flesh too which works wonderfully for flavouring alcoholic drinks and desserts such as baked goods and ice cream. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including bitter orange creme brulee!
As well as being versatile, flying dragon oranges are nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are excellent sources of vitamin C and are rich in vitamin A, potassium, and calcium.

Due to this eye-catching appearance, the fruit trees are highly regarded as an ornamental variety for private and public gardens, once being planted in the gardens of St Paul's Cathedral!
Flying dragons are native to China and Korea, however they are today cultivated around the world. They are small in size - typically measuring only 3-4cm in diameter! - and round in shape. They have a pebbled, orange rind that has a slightly velvety feel due to their downy coating. Beneath their textured skin is thin, white, spongy pith, attached to tender, yellow flesh that emits a glorious citrus fragrance and is sure to wow your tastebuds: the soft, seeded flesh is exceptionally juicy and intensely tart, astounding eaters with its combination of lemon-like tanginess and bitter notes of grapefruit. These acidic fruits have therefore earned the name 'bitter oranges'!
Like other citrus fruits, flying dragon oranges are not typically eaten fresh out of hand due to their sharp savour and little flesh content. Instead, they are primarily cooked to make delectable marmalades, syrups, jams, and jellies, and are often candied with sugar to create scrumptious chewy snacks! The peels can also be zested like lemons and limes to flavour everything from cakes to cocktails, garnish cocktails (and mocktails!), and create perfect seasoning powder by drying and grinding. A small amount of juice can be extracted from the flesh too which works wonderfully for flavouring alcoholic drinks and desserts such as baked goods and ice cream. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including bitter orange creme brulee!
As well as being versatile, flying dragon oranges are nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are excellent sources of vitamin C and are rich in vitamin A, potassium, and calcium.

Name: Citrus - grapefruit, pink
Description:
One of the most popular citrus fruits, grapefruits are an absolute must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Our pink grapefruits are medium to large in size and round - almost perfectly spherical! - in shape. They have attractive golden-orange peel that is smooth, glossy, and semi-thin and is covered with small oil glands that release a delightful floral aroma!
Beneath this fragrant skin is thick, white pith that is bitter and spongy. The pith is attached to segmented flesh that dazzles the eye with its vibrant reddish-pink hue. This tender flesh is supremely succulent, bursting with juice, and boasts a complex flavour profile that combines bright and sweet notes with acidic and tangy undertones!
Although pink grapefruits' sweet-tart flesh is usually simply scooped out and eaten off the spoon, it is also perfect for use in any number of recipes! Ideal for incorporating into fruit and green salads, the flesh is also delectable when blended into smoothies, juiced into cocktails, and chopped into salsas. They are additionally splendid flavouring ingredients, working brilliantly well in imparting tropical notes in baked goods, sauces, and sorbets! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including grapefruit margaritas!
As well as being delicious and versatile, pink grapefruits are also nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and are rich in dietary fibre and vitamin A. Our dried pink grapefruit is washed, sliced and dehydrated. There are no added ingredients. Steep it in hot water to make a citrus tea, use in distilling, mix with water and sugar to make your own pink grapefruit syrup, or use for garnishing! For a fruit that is similar to grapefruit, but with a sweeter flavour, we recommend our honey pomelo!

Name: Citrus - kabosu
Description:
Kabosu is a highly-prized citrus delicacy!
Kabosus are small, round - they are almost perfectly spherical! - citrus fruits that originate from Japan. They have eye-catching dark green peel (ripening to a bright yellow when the fruits are fully ripe) that is smooth, glossy, and covered in small oil glands that emit an intense floral aroma that fills the room!
Beneath this attractive, semi-thin skin is a layer of white, spongy pith that is directly attached to segmented pale yellow flesh. The seeded flesh of kabosu is tender and supremely succulent, almost bursting with juice! This juicy flesh wows the tastebuds with its complex flavour profile: primarily tart and sour in savour, it imparts subtle notes of sweetness too, and impresses with its hints of lemon, mint, and melon.
Closely related to yuzu citrus, it's not surprising that kabosu is similarly perfect for adding a kick of flavour to food and drink recipes! Although in their native Japan kabosu is principally valued for the way its juice mellows the marine-like taste of fish dishes, this acidic juice is extremely versatile. You can use it to create bright, sour-tasting sauces, dressings, and marinades; incorporate it into soups and curries, and infuse it into marmalades, pastries, and even ice cream! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including a scrumptious kabosu lime pie!
As well as being packed full of flavour, kabosus are also nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are rich in vitamin C and are a good source of potassium and folate.

Name: Citrus - kumquat, honey kumquat
Description:
Love kumquats? Our new honey kumquats are just the thing for you!
Our honey kumquats (also known as 'crispy honey kumquats') from Rong'an County, Guangxi in China have a similar appearance to regular kumquats, which somewhat resemble small oranges - the name kumquat comes from the Cantonese term, 'kam kwat', meaning 'golden orange'! - however they are slightly larger and more rounded than other kumquats (which tend to be oval and olive-sized).
These kumquats are regarded by many people as having a superior taste to their sister fruits. Whilst we love the unique flavour combination of regular kumquats, which have sharp flesh and sweet skin, we equally adore the taste of honey kumquats. When you peel back the thin, smooth, golden-orange skin of these fruits, your tastebuds are wowed by the supremely crisp and juicy flesh (which is often completely seedless). Their fragrant, white/cream-coloured flesh is sweeter and far less sour than other kumquats: as their name suggests, these delightful fruits have a sweet taste reminiscent of honey, so they are ideal for those with a sweet tooth! Indeed, they're so sweet that they have been nicknamed the 'small sugar cannons' of the kumquat family!
These delectable, succulent fruits are best enjoyed fresh out of hand - simply wash the fruits, then devour them! However, honey kumquats are also well suited to a number of culinary applications. We'd recommend using them in recipes that call for regular kumquats. Their sweetness means they are particularly ideal for making mouthwatering desserts such as kumquat sorbet! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration!
As well as being delicious, honey kumquats boast a range of nutritional benefits. Like regular kumquats, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and dietary fibre, and contain good amounts of vitamin A and calcium.

Ingredients

  • 2 cups of kumquats, chopped
  • 1/2 cup sugar
  • 1/2 water
  • Spices such as vanilla bean or cinammon

Method

  1. Place the kumquats, sugar, and spices in a saucepan. Let it sit for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally.
  2. Add water and bring to a boil over high heat. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer for 15-20 minutes or until the liquid has reduced and thickened.
  3. Place in an airtight container and store in a refrigerator. Use within 2 weeks.

Our honey kumquats (also known as 'crispy honey kumquats') from Rong'an County, Guangxi in China have a similar appearance to regular kumquats, which somewhat resemble small oranges - the name kumquat comes from the Cantonese term, 'kam kwat', meaning 'golden orange'! - however they are slightly larger and more rounded than other kumquats (which tend to be oval and olive-sized).
These kumquats are regarded by many people as having a superior taste to their sister fruits. Whilst we love the unique flavour combination of regular kumquats, which have sharp flesh and sweet skin, we equally adore the taste of honey kumquats. When you peel back the thin, smooth, golden-orange skin of these fruits, your tastebuds are wowed by the supremely crisp and juicy flesh (which is often completely seedless). Their fragrant, white/cream-coloured flesh is sweeter and far less sour than other kumquats: as their name suggests, these delightful fruits have a sweet taste reminiscent of honey, so they are ideal for those with a sweet tooth! Indeed, they're so sweet that they have been nicknamed the 'small sugar cannons' of the kumquat family!
These delectable, succulent fruits are best enjoyed fresh out of hand - simply wash the fruits, then devour them! However, honey kumquats are also well suited to a number of culinary applications. We'd recommend using them in recipes that call for regular kumquats. Their sweetness means they are particularly ideal for making mouthwatering desserts such as kumquat sorbet! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration!
As well as being delicious, honey kumquats boast a range of nutritional benefits. Like regular kumquats, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and dietary fibre, and contain good amounts of vitamin A and calcium.

Name: Citrus - lemon, Amalfi, unwaxed
Description:
Looking for a fruit to provide an intense citrus kick to your favourite dishes? Amalfi lemons are just the thing for you!
Native to the scenic Amalfi Coast in Italy, Amalfi lemons are one of the most popular varieties of citrus fruit in Italy and for good reason - they stand out in their delightfully fragrant aroma, abundant juice, and spectacular flavour.
As well as being large in size - they are significantly bigger than supermarket-bought lemons! - Amalfi lemons are also renowned for their distinctive shape, being much more elongated and tapered than the rounder lemons commonly cultivated in Italy.
Amalfi lemons have glossy, yellow peel that immediately attracts the eye. Beneath this bumpy, semi-thick skin is bright white, spongy pith and tender, golden-yellow flesh that will wow your tastebuds: it is supremely succulent and tart with delicate undertones of sweetness. These lemons typically contain a few small seeds encased in their flesh.
Favoured by chefs, our Amalfi lemons are exceedingly refreshing, and their acidic flesh makes their juice the perfect flavouring - they are renowned for having a perfectly balanced juice - whether you are marinading meat or fish, making jams or marmalades, or creating cocktails. Indeed, Amalfi lemons are regarded as the best lemons to use when making limoncello! Whatever you choose, this lemon juice will provide the ideal burst of citrus goodness to anything you desire!
There are more ways to enjoy Amalfi lemons beyond juicing, though! For example, many people are not aware that lemon peel is not only edible, but it is supremely delicious and packed full of nutrients! The peel of Amalfi lemons is extremely aromatic and tangy, and as such, is a wonderful flavouring for creams, liqueurs, cocktails and mocktails, desserts, and more. Their richness in healthy essential oils makes them even more appealing! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite lemon recipes, including a scrumptious lemon and almond cake!
Alongside being packed full of flavour and extremely versatile, Amalfi lemons also offer great nutritional value. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C - they contain even more vitamin C than other lemon varieties! - dietary fibre, and folate, the latter of which is vital for developing healthy red blood cells. Among a range of vitamins and minerals, including potassium and magnesium, these splendid fruits also contain limonene, a natural compound with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.

Name: Citrus - lemon, Caribbean rough lemon
Description:
Our rough lemons are a rare and unique seeded citrus organically grown on a farm in St Lucia and harvested in the winter months.
The eye-catching uneven exterior is the reason for this variety also being known as 'rough lemon' or 'coarse lemon'.
They are popular across the Caribbean for their thick zest and aromatic juice, which once ripe, is sweeter than other lemon varieties. Being sweeter than the usual commercially available lemons, but still having the usual sour, tart lemon flavour and aroma, rough lemons make a superior lemon juice.
The rough lemons will ripen from green to orange and can be used at all stages of ripeness.
Rough lemons are around two to three times the size of a typical supermarket bought lemon here in the UK.
Some gardeners cultvate rough lemons next to the more attractive meyer lemon, a combination known as 'Beauty and the Beast'.

Our jara lemons are mostly sour with a hint of sweetness. The smell of a jara lemon is highly aromatic and sweet.
The jara lemon originates from Bangladesh, where it has been said to be one of the top ranking countries for cultivating the lemon tree!
Looks are deceiving, this unique citrus is neither a lime or lemon species!
It is only in recent years that the jara lemon has become available to foreign countries, a farmer in Sylhet said "We're cultivating jara Lemon commercially now but our ancestors used to produce it only to meet the family need."

Name: Citrus - lemon, meyer lemon
Description:
A cross between a lemon and a mandarin orange, Meyer lemons are a must-try for citrus lovers!
These fruits first cultivated in China resemble other lemon varieties in appearance: they have smooth, golden yellow peel and are round to oval in shape.
Beneath their delicate, supremely aromatic (and edible!) skin is a layer of white pith that is so thin that Meyer lemons may be eaten in their entirety! Not only do Meyer lemons stand out in that they are completely edible: their tender, yellow flesh wows eaters with its distinctive sweet flavour! Unlike other lemons, this often seedless variety possesses little acidity, so the flesh has a sugary taste perfect for those with a sweet tooth!
The bright, floral flavour of Meyer lemons means they are ideal for use in any number of sweet and savoury dishes - Meyer lemons can be used anywhere you want to add pure lemon flavour with none of the characteristic lemon bitterness! We'd recommend cutting thin slices of lemon, removing the seeds, and roasting the slices with root vegetables or seafood. In sweet foods such as marmalade or lemonade, the lower acid level of Meyer lemons means less sugar may be required! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including Meyer lemon marshmallows!
As well as being delicious and versatile, Meyer lemons boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin C and are rich in potassium.
