Name: Pear - nashi
Description:
Nashi pears, also known as Asian pears, are delicious fruits that have been popular in many Asian cuisines for centuries but that don't get enough recognition in the UK!
Round in shape and about the same size as an apple, Nashi pears are distinct firstly in their appearance: white speckles are set against pale orange skin (which is edible), making for a delightful sight.
Beneath this attractive skin is firm white flesh, which is refreshingly crisp, fresh, subtly sweet, and supremely succulent - their high quantity of juice makes them a real thirst quencher! Some people compare the flavour of Nashi pears to a unique combination of apple and pear.
These crunchy, sweet fruits are best eaten fresh out of hand, consumed like you would an apple or a pear - peel it (if you desire), and then cut into wedges and enjoy! However, they are also ideal for use in a variety of sweet and savoury recipes. For example, you could serve them slightly chilled and pair them with cheese; bake them into tarts and pies, or use them to make a revitalizing juice! Additionally, it is popular to poach Nashi pears - check out the 'Further information' tab below for an amazing recipe for poached Nashi pear with cinnamon yoghurt!
As well as being delectable and versatile, Nashi pears also boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are rich in vitamins C and K and provide a good amount of dietary fibre.

Name: Pear - piqaboo
Description:
Are you a pear lover looking for a new variety to enjoy? If so, we have just the thing for you!
PiqaBoo pears are wonderful fruits first developed in New Zealand. Created by crossing an Asian and European pear, these relatively new fruits bring together the best features of these distinct varieties: they boast the more intense, and often more complex, flavours of European pears, the crisp texture of Japanese types, and the longer shelf-life of Chinese varieties.
Small to medium in size and having the typical pear shape, PiqaBoo pears have a dazzling appearance, immediately catching your eye with their glossy, bright red and brown speckled skin. Their skin is also distinctive in that when they mature, they produce a natural wax which protects the fruit from scuffing, meaning that they last longer in your fridge or fruit bowl.
Their flavour is divine, with white flesh that is exquisitely crisp, succulent, and refreshing, and the pears particularly delight the tastebuds with their glorious sweetness (owing to the fact that they have a low acidity in comparison to other pears).
Although best enjoyed simply eaten fresh out of hand, they are also ideal for use in a variety of food and drink creations. Indeed, they work well in any recipe where pears are featured! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for two of our favourite recipes, including one for mini PiqaBoo pear tarts, the perfect sweet treat for all the family!
As well as being delicious and versatile, PiqaBoo pears provide a range of health benefits. Like all pears, they are an excellent source of vitamins C and K and are rich in fibre and potassium. Uniquely, however, PiqaBoo pears are believed to contain properties that help cure hangovers! The image used in this listing is with credit to www.goldenbayfruit.com

Name: Peppercorn - green peppercorn, fresh
Description:
Green peppercorns are perfect for adding a kick of heat to your mealtimes!
They are the same berry as black peppercorns - they are green in colour because they are picked before fully ripening. However, they still have a wonderful fresh aroma and a delicious flavour: they have a less intense taste, so are better for those who are not as keen on spiciness, and some people prefer green peppercorns to black or white peppercorns because their gentle heat and peppery tang is complemented by a subtle fruitiness that gives them a more complex flavour.
Green peppercorns can be enjoyed in many different ways, and are becoming as popular in European cuisine as they are in Thai and Vietnamese dishes. For the best flavour, we recommend using them in dishes with a short cooking time because this will preserve their delicious fresh flavour. They pair particularly well with duck and game, and are ideal for making the famous sauce au poivre vert, in English simply 'green peppercorn sauce', a rich cream sauce that is usually served with steak. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes!
As well as bursting with flavour, green peppercorns are also nutritionally valuable, being a good source of vitamins C, A, and K and rich in various antioxidants.

Name: Persimmon
Description:
Persimmon are an absolute must-try for all exotic fruit lovers!
Stripped of all astringency, Persimmon are small, wonderfully sweet, orange-red fruits originating from Asia, believed to first be cultivated in China in the 7th century (China is still today the largest producer of them!) Cultivation expanded into Japan and Korea, where over 2,000 varieties or cultivars are now listed, they arrived in Europe between the 17th and 19th centuries, and have since become a global phenomenon - did you know that each year around 5 billion kilos of Persimmon are harvested?
We source our Persimmon from Spain and Brazil. Our 'triumph' and 'rojo brillante' varieties are both grown in Spain, with the most important plantations concentrated in the province of Valencia, in the riverside towns on the Xuquer river, particularly Carlet and Alginet. Cultivation of Persimmon in Spain is agriculturally significant, and the rojo brillante persimmon from Ribera del Xúquer has its own D.O.P. (Protected Designation of Origin): farmers in this region have carefully cultivated the fruits using natural techniques since the late 1990s, in order to develop this non-astringent variety.
Popular with growers all over the world, people often at first sight mistake Persimmon for a flat tomato. However, even if in appearance they resemble tomatoes, once you've sampled their juicy flesh you will know you're consuming something totally different! Beneath their glossy, smooth skin is pale orange flesh that ripens from firm and crisp to mouthwateringly succulent and tender, with a complex flavour that delights the tastebuds: within the glorious sweetness are wonderful hints of brown sugar, peach and mango combine to make an amazing taste sensation!
Although best enjoyed simply eaten fresh out of hand, they are very versatile, being suited to a range of culinary applications whether they are firm and dense or have the softness and squishiness of full maturity. We'd especially recommend cooking them into jams and chutneys, adding slices to fruit salads, chopping them into salsas, and incorporating them into sweet baked goods such as tarts and pies! You can even dry them to turn them into a chewy snack! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes, including Persimmon chiffon pie!
As well as being delicious, Persimmon boast a range of nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre, vitamin C, and magnesium, and are rich in many nutrients, including copper, iron, calcium, and phosphorus.

Name: Persimmon, dried (China) - sweet and sticky
Description:
Looking for a new dried fruit to try? We have just the thing for you: 100% pure dried persimmon
Dried persimmons are a popular snack throughout Asia, and are considered a delicacy in Japanese cuisine due to their limited quantities and labour-intensive process of creation. Indeed, the fruits have long been held in high acclaim - during the Han Dynasty in China, for instance, dried persimmons were so highly regarded that they were commonly given as gifts to the imperial court!
Our dried persimmons from China differ from the more well-known dried persimmons from Turkey and Japan. Whereas the latter are oval-shaped, brown fruits with a wrinkled, textured surface, our Chinese dried persimmons are round and almost resemble doughnuts in shape, and dazzle the eye with their intriguing red colour.
The flesh has an intriguing texture, one that we would describe as soft and chewy with a sticky centre. The taste is wonderful, and will be an instant hit for those of you with a sweet tooth! Your tastebuds will be delighted by the delicious sweetness of the fruit's natural sugar content, complemented by a delightful fruitiness and hints of brown sugar and cinnamon. Being small in size and ready to eat, they make the perfect snack!
As well as being delectable, dried persimmons boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin A and are rich in dietary fibre, and with no preservatives, additives or flavourings added in, you can also be comfortable in knowing that you're consuming only pure fruit.

Name: Persimmon, dried (Turkey) - sweet and sticky
Description:
Looking for a new dried fruit to try? We have just the thing for you!
Our dried persimmon, also known as Hoshigaki persimmon, is a popular snack throughout Asia, and is considered a delicacy in Japanese cuisine due to their limited quantities and labour-intensive process of creation. Indeed, the fruits have long been held in high acclaim - during the Han Dynasty in China, for instance, dried persimmons were so highly regarded that they were commonly given as gifts to the imperial court!
These oval-shaped, brown fruits have a wrinkled, textured surface, delicately covered with a light white coating of sugar that the fruits naturally develop when they are ready for consumption.
The flesh has an intriguing texture, one that we would describe as chewy, sticky, and gummy, comparable in some ways to hard jelly. The taste is wonderful, and will be an instant hit for those of you with a sweet tooth! Your tastebuds will be dazzled by the delicious caramelised sugary flavour, a sweet and fruity flavour taste with glorious undertones of honey, brown sugar and cinnamon. They make the perfect snack for when you crave something that's both healthy and sweet!
Most often eaten out of hand, dried persimmons are also used throughout Asia as sweeteners for beverages - the fruits are favoured for making tea and wine - baked goods, and appetisers. In Korea, dried persimmons are stuffed with pine nuts and served with confectionary, and they are also simmered into sujonggwa, a ginger and cinnamon punch usually served during festive periods.
As well as being delectable, dried persimmon boast many nutritional benefits. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamin A and are rich in dietary fibre. Dried persimmon are the result of a complex process of peeling, hang-drying and daily hand-massaging the persimmon fruit (also known as sharon fruit), and no preservatives, additives or flavourings are added in, so you can also be comfortable in knowing that you're consuming only pure fruit.

Name: Pomegranate
Description:
Pomegranates are a must-try for all fruit lovers!
Round in shape and medium in size, our pomegranates from Peru somewhat resemble apples in appearance. However, what's underneath the surface makes pomegranates stand out from the crowd. Beneath their smooth, glossy red skin is an abundance of white seeds encased in ruby-red sacs! These sacs, known as arils, are not only completely eye-catching - they almost look like jewels! - but the flesh contained in them is also supremely delicious. The skin and pith should not be eaten.
Once you've removed the sacs from the pith, the succulent flesh can be eaten raw - the arils have a taste similar to cranberries, with a sharpness complemented by delicate notes of sweetness. The arils are also commonly juiced to make a refreshing beverage. Although these are the two most typical uses, pomegranates can be used in any number of recipes. We'd particularly recommend scattering the sacs over cereals and oatmeal, incorporating them in salads, and using them to decorate meat and fish dishes. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes, including an orange and pomegranate cheesecake!
As well as being delectable and versatile, pomegranates have in recent years become renowned for their nutritional benefits. Commonly regarded as a super food, they are packed with antioxidants and are an excellent source of dietary fibre.

Name: Potato - Arran Victory
Description:
Arran victory potatoes are one of the fluffiest, tastiest potatoes that we sell!
Hailing from the Scottish Isle of Arran, this heritage variety began to be cultivated in the early 20th century and commercially released in 1918 to celebrate the victory of the Allied powers in World War One (hence the 'victory' part of their name).
These potatoes vary in size and shape, ranging from small to medium and round to oval depending on soil quality and climate. They have visually appealing purple-coloured skin that's delicate, smooth, and thin, and dense, firm flesh that, once cooked, has a tender, buttery texture - the particularly high starch content of Arran victory potatoes means the flesh is better at absorbing moisture, so they have a velvet-smooth texture superior to most other types of potatoes! - and a flavour that is fresh, earthy, and nutty.
Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, Arran victory potatoes' especially fluffy flesh makes them particularly well suited to roasting, mashing, and baking. We would also recommend honouring their Scottish roots by pairing them with haggis, and using them to make 'rumbledethumps', a traditional dish consisting of potato, onion, and cabbage that is as hearty and comforting as it is delightfully named. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for these recipes, as well as a recipe for an especially delectable shepherd's pie!
Like other potatoes, Arran victory potatoes are an excellent source of fibre and potassium, and also provide good amounts of iron, folate, and vitamins C and B6.

Tab Content:Preparation:
Wash well before use.

Cook before eating.
Tab Content:Usage: Use as you would any other potato: boil, steam, fry, bake etc. Arran victory potatoes' fluffy nature means they are best suited to baking, mashing, and roasting.
Tab Content:Storage: Arran victory potatoes will keep up to two weeks when stored in a cool, dry, and dark location.
Tab Content:Further Info:
Wondering how best to enjoy your Arran victory potatoes? We recommend using them to make this delicious haggis shepherd's pie, a hearty meal perfect for any evening (but especially so on Burn's Night!), and this traditional Scottish rumbledethumps, a scrumptious, unique dish!

Arran victory potatoes also make a delectable shepherd's pie - below is the recipe.

Ingredients

  • 500g Arran victory potatoes
  • 500g sweded
  • 500g haggis
  • 2tbsp rapesed oil
  • 1 onion, chopped
  • 2 cloves of garlic, minced
  • 400ml vegetable stock
  • 200g frozen peas
  • Butter, milk, and salt (optional)

Method

  1. Preheat the over to 180 degrees celsius (160 degrees for fan ovens/Gas Mark 4).
  2. Peel the potatoes and swede and cut into roughly even-sized chunks.
  3. Boil the potatoes with a pinch of salt for 15 minutes (or until cooked through).
  4. In a pan, heat the oil and gently cook the onion garlic until they start to brown. Crumble in the haggis, add the stock, and then add the peas.
  5. Leave to simmer for 10-15 minutes (or until the mixture begins to thicken).
  6. Drain the potatoes and swede and mash thoroughly, adding butter and milk as required.
  7. Transfer the haggis mixture to an oven dish, top with the mash, and cook in the over for 30 minutes or until golden brown and crispy!

Blue Anneliese gratin

Ingredients:

  • 700g Blue Anneliese potatoes
  • 125g cheddar cheese, grated
  • 150ml single cream
  • 2 large tomatoes
  • Salt and ground black pepper

Method:

  1. Preheat the oven to 200°C.
  2. Lightly grease an ovenproof dish.
  3. Slice the potatoes thinly and cover the base of the dish with a layer of these.
  4. Alternately layer the potato, slices of tomato and cheese, seasoning as you go. Finish with a layer of potato and pour over the cream and sprinkle grated cheese on top.
  5. Cook for 1-1 1/2 hours, or until the potatoes are tender.

Duchess potatoes

Ingredients:

250g Blue Anneliese potatoes

Knob of butter

20ml of milk

Edible sugarcraft eyes

Method:

  1. Preheat the oven to 180°C.
  2. Line 1 baking tray.
  3. Peel the potatoes and place them in a saucepan with cold water. Boil for approximately 15 minutes, until the potatoes are tender.
  4. Drain the potatoes.
  5. Mash the potatoes with butter and milk (or cold-pressed rapeseed oil) until smooth.
  6. Prepare your piping bag with a star or round nozzle. Spoon some of the mashed potatoes into the piping bag and, on a lined baking tree, pipe some swirly pyramids. Decorate with the sugarcraft eyes by firmly pressing them into the potato.
  7. Place in the oven for 5-10 minutes until the potato begins to turn golden.

Rosemary and garlic roast potatoes with chipolatas

Ingredients:

  • 2kg desiree potatoes, cut into large pieces
  • 2 tbsp butter
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 1 bulb garlic, separated into unpeeled cloves
  • 2 tbsp chopped rosemary
  • 12 pork chipolatas

Method:

  1. Heat oven to 200°C.
  2. Put the potatoes in a pan of cold water, bring to the boil and simmer for 5 minutes.
  3. Meanwhile, put the butter and oil into a large, shallow roasting tray and heat in the oven. 
  4. Drain the potatoes in a colander, giving them a good shake to fluff the edges up a little.
  5. Toss the hot oil in the tray and roast for 20 minutes.
  6. Add the garlic, rosemary and chipolatas to the tray, mix together and roast for a further 50 minutes until the potatoes are crunchy and golden brown and the sausages are cooked through.

Heide Red rose dauphinoise recipe

Ingredients:

  • 500g Heide red potatoes
  • 200ml double cream
  • Knob of butter
  • Salt to taste

Method:

  1. Preheat the oven to 170°C and grease a muffin tin with the butter.
  2. Slice the potatoes into very thin rounds using a mandoline or knife. 
  3. Arrange the slices in the tin, starting by lining the outside edge of each case and slightly overlapping until you reach the middle and have created a flower of potato petals.
  4. Pour a little cream into the centre of each flower and sprinkle with salt to season. 
  5. Place in the over and cook for 45 minutes or until the potatoes are tender. Turn the oven up to 200°C for 10 minutes to crisp the tips of the petals.

Name: Potato - Jersey Royal
Description:
Jersey Royal potatoes are one of the best potato varieties we've tried!
Grown exclusively on the island of Jersey for over 140 years - over half of the land on Jersey used to be devoted solely to growing these potatoes! - Jersey Royal potatoes are renowned for their flavour. The farmers believe their excellent sweet yet earthy flavour comes from the way they are grown: not only are they cultivated on steep fields along the coast, meaning they benefit from a combination of sunshine, salty breezes, and a mild climate, but the growers fertilize the fields with a local seaweed which is believed to enhance their rich flavour.
From appearance alone, you would not have guessed that Jersey Royal potatoes are often called 'the champagne of potatoes', in reference to the robust protections in place to ensure they achieve the highest standard and quality. They are relatively small in size and long or oval in shape, and have pale yellow to light brown skin. Beneath their delicate, flaky skin, however, is supremely delectable, firm, cream-coloured flesh that, once cooked, is tender, sweet, and earthy. We particularly noted their distinctly nutty undertones and wonderful freshness. They're only in season for a very short time, so make sure to buy them while you can!
Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, Jersey Royal potatoes are especially well suited to roasting, boiling, and baking. Why not follow local Jersey tradition and boil them in salt water before serving them with fresh mint and butter? They are also ideal for adding some subtle sweetness to salads, curries, and soups, and we'd recommend using them to make hearty shepherd pies and incorporating slices into gratins and casseroles. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including mouthwateringly tasty Jersey Royal crab cakes!
Like other potatoes, Jersey Royal potatoes are an excellent source of fibre and potassium, and also provide good amounts of iron, folate, and vitamins C and B6.

Name: Potato - la ratte
Description:
La ratte potatoes are one of Europe's most sought-after gourmet potato varieties - indeed, in their native France they have gained the nickname 'la reine', meaning 'the queen'!
Although first cultivated in the 19th century, these small to medium, oblong-shaped potatoes did not have much commercial success until the 1960s, when top French chefs selected them as their choice potatoes for fine dining recipes: Michelin star restaurants still today favour la ratte potatoes due to their superior flavour and texture.
We too find the firm yellow flesh (concealed beneath la ratte potatoes' delicate golden skin) especially delicious - once cooked, the flesh has a texture that is as smooth as butter and a delectable flavour that can be described as earthy with nutty undertones and a very subtle sweetness.
Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, la ratte potatoes are particularly well suited for boiling, braising, and roasting, and they make a spectacularly creamy mash. After being boiled and pureed they are also ideal bases for sauces and soups. We would recommend using them to make scrumptious roast potatoes, a healthy but filling potato salad, and a delectable la ratte tartiflette - check out the 'Further information' tab below for the recipes!
Like other potatoes, la ratte potatoes are an excellent source of fibre and potassium, and also provide a good amount of vitamin C.

Wondering how best to enjoy your la ratte potatoes? We recommend using them to make these delicious roast potatoes infused with wild garlic pesto and this healthy but filling potato salad!

We'd also suggest making a delectable tartiflette - below is the recipe.

Ingredients

  • 1kg la ratte potatoes
  • 250g smoked bacon lardons
  • 200ml double cream
  • 100ml white wine
  • 450g Reblochon cheese
  • 2 shallots
  • 1 garlic clove

Method

  1. Preheat the over to 200 degrees celsius (180 degrees in a fan oven/Gas Mark 4)
  2. Cook the potatoes in salted water for 5-10 minutes, or until tender. Drain and set aside to steam dry.
  3. Fry the bacon, shallots, and garlic in a pin for 4-5 minutes, or until golden brown. Add the white wine and cook until evaporated.
  4. Slice the potatoes thinly and alternately layer in an oven proof dish with the bacon mixture. Pour the double cream over the top, season with salt and pepper, and finish with a layer of the sliced Reblochon cheese.
  5. Bake in the over for 10-15 minutes or until the cheese is golden brown and bubbling.

Description:
Pink fir apple potatoes are a must-try!
These elongated potatoes, which are native to France (introduced to Britain in the 1850s), have smooth, semi-thick skin that can vary in colour from cream to light brown with pink blushing. Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, pink fir apple potatoes are renowned for how they retain their shape even when cooked, and are usually cooked with their skin. We'd recommend using them as a salad potato, boiling and mixing them with fresh herbs, greens, and sauces, and slicing them to make gourmet chips! You can also boil and lightly mash them with some salted butter to create heavenly mashed potatoes. Pink fir apple potatoes pair well with apples, tomatoes, beets, spinach, herbs, mozzarella, legumes, leeks, capers, mackerel, and other meats such as poultry and steak. Like other potatoes, pink fir apples potatoes are an excellent source of fibre and potassium, and also provide good amounts of iron, folate, and vitamins C and B6.

  • Handful of wild garlic leaves, chopped
  • 1 large onion, peeled and finely chopped
  • 1.5L chicken stock
  • Knob of butter
  • Salt and pepper

Name: Potato - purple, 'violetta', 'valfi' & 'vitelotte'
Description:
Vitelotte, violetta, and valfi potatoes are some of the most visually appealing and nutritionally valuable potato varieties that we sell!
These purple potatoes, which owe their name to their dazzling deep purple/dark blue skin and flesh, are regarded by many as gourmet delicacies - indeed, vitelotte potatoes are so rare and highly prized that they have gained the nickname 'truffle potatoes'!
They all are generally medium in size (although vitelotte can sometimes be smaller) and they all have flesh that, concealed beneath smooth (violetta) or bumpy (valfi and vitelotte) skin, has a denser texture and a slightly nuttier, earthier flavour than a white potato. Once cooked, the flesh of all three varieties is floury yet smooth (violettas have the fluffiest texture of the three), and has a delicious flavour somewhat reminiscent of chestnuts. If you are looking for a sweeter potato, we would recommend the violetta, as these have subtle undertones of sweetness, whereas if you are looking for a potato with a more distinctive, spicier flavour we would suggest choosing valfi potatoes.
Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, purple potatoes are very versatile and will suit all of your culinary needs. However, they are arguably most well-suited for boiling, mashing, baking, and frying; we would recommend keeping the skins on during cooking so you can retain the eye-catching colour! As the flesh retains much of its vibrant purple hue even once cooked, purple potatoes are perfect for adding some colour to your mealtimes - we would suggest making spectacular purple roast and mashed potatoes; adding purple potato to your salads to boost their healthiness; making use of their drier texture to make potato pancakes and gnocchi, and boiling and pureeing them to make purple soup. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes - we would especially suggest the violetta gratin and smashed vitelotte potatoes recipes!
Vitelotte, violetta, and valfi potatoes stand out in terms of their health benefits. As well as being, like other potatoes, an excellent source of fibre and potassium, and a good provider of iron, folate, and vitamins C and B6, these potatoes are also uniquely rich in anti-oxidants - valfi potatoes contain around 30% more anti-oxidants than white potatoes! - such as anthocyanin, which is believed to boost the immune system.

  • 125g cheddar cheese, grated
  • 150ml single cream
  • 2 large tomatoes
  • Salt and ground black pepper

Method

  1. Preheat the oven to 200°C (180° for fan ovens/Gas Mark 6).
  2. Lightly grease an oven-proof dish.
  3. Slice the potatoes thinly and cover the base of the dish with a layer of these.
  4. Alternately layer the potato, slices of tomato and cheese, seasoning as you go. Finish with a layer of potato and pour over the cream and sprinkle some cheese on the top.
  5. Cook for 1 to 1 and a half hours, or until the potatoes are tender.

Why not also make these wonderful smashed vitelotte potatoes?

Ingredients

  • 1kg vitelotte potatoes
  • 3-4tbsp olive oil
  • 1 clove of garlic
  • Thyme, parsley, salt, pepper
  • Handful of pine nuts

Method

  1. Boil the potatoes in salty water for about 20 minutes or until they are fork-tender. Drain them and let them cool for a few minutes.
  2. Preheat the oven to 200°C. 
  3. Arrange the potatoes on a baking tray and smash them using a cup or glass or a small bowl.
  4. Mix the olive oil with the crushed garlic and spices, and drizzle the potatoes with the mixture.
  5. Bake them for about 20 minutes, then garnish with herbs and nuts. Enjoy!

Name: Potato - purple, 'violetta', 'valfi' & 'vitelotte'
Description:
Vitelotte, violetta, and valfi potatoes are some of the most visually appealing and nutritionally valuable potato varieties that we sell!
These purple potatoes, which owe their name to their dazzling deep purple/dark blue skin and flesh, are regarded by many as gourmet delicacies - indeed, vitelotte potatoes are so rare and highly prized that they have gained the nickname 'truffle potatoes'!
They all are generally medium in size (although vitelotte can sometimes be smaller) and they all have flesh that, concealed beneath smooth (violetta) or bumpy (valfi and vitelotte) skin, has a denser texture and a slightly nuttier, earthier flavour than a white potato. Once cooked, the flesh of all three varieties is floury yet smooth (violettas have the fluffiest texture of the three), and has a delicious flavour somewhat reminiscent of chestnuts. If you are looking for a sweeter potato, we would recommend the violetta, as these have subtle undertones of sweetness, whereas if you are looking for a potato with a more distinctive, spicier flavour we would suggest choosing valfi potatoes.
Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, purple potatoes are very versatile and will suit all of your culinary needs. However, they are arguably most well-suited for boiling, mashing, baking, and frying; we would recommend keeping the skins on during cooking so you can retain the eye-catching colour! As the flesh retains much of its vibrant purple hue even once cooked, purple potatoes are perfect for adding some colour to your mealtimes - we would suggest making spectacular purple roast and mashed potatoes; adding purple potato to your salads to boost their healthiness; making use of their drier texture to make potato pancakes and gnocchi, and boiling and pureeing them to make purple soup. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipes - we would especially suggest the violetta gratin and smashed vitelotte potatoes recipes!
Vitelotte, violetta, and valfi potatoes stand out in terms of their health benefits. As well as being, like other potatoes, an excellent source of fibre and potassium, and a good provider of iron, folate, and vitamins C and B6, these potatoes are also uniquely rich in anti-oxidants - valfi potatoes contain around 30% more anti-oxidants than white potatoes! - such as anthocyanin, which is believed to boost the immune system.

Name: Potato - Red Duke of York
Description:
Red Duke of York potatoes are one of the fluffiest potato varieties you can buy!
First cultivated in the UK in 1942, these potatoes were a favourite among home gardeners during World War Two and have been popular ever since.
This medium to large, oval-shaped variety has dazzling deep red skin that's delicate, smooth, and thin, and firm cream-coloured flesh that, once cooked, has a tender and delightfully fluffy texture. Indeed, their flesh has such a high content of dry matter that they are regarded by many chefs as the fluffiest potatoes! This delicious flesh has a fresh, earthy flavour.
Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, Red Duke of York potatoes are perfect for roasting - make sure to keep the skins on during cooking so you can retain the eye-catching colour and wow your family and friends with red-skinned roast potatoes! They are also ideal for mashing and making heavenly fluffy gnocchi. Indeed, they are a great all-rounder - there are so many ways you can use them to add some colour and sweetness to your mealtimes, from boiling to wedging to using them as salad potatoes. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes!
Red Duke of York potatoes boast a number of health benefits. Like other potatoes, they are an excellent source of fibre and potassium, and a good provider of iron, folate, and vitamins C and B6.

Name: Potato - russet burbank
Description:
First cultivated in Idaho in 1914, russet burbank potatoes have since become a favourite all over America.
In the UK too they are very popular, and for good reason. Medium in size and oval in shape, russet burbanks have light brown skin and firm white flesh that, once cooked, has a smooth texture and a deliciously buttery flavour with mildly earthy undertones.
Consumed in a similar way to other potato varieties, russet burbanks' floury texture means they are perfect for baking, mashing, and roasting - they make especially delectable chips and wedges! We would particularly recommend using them to make a crispy hasselback potato gratin, a hearty and comforting accompaniment to your meals, and heavenly fluffy mashed potatoes. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including russet burbank American-style fries!
Like other potatoes, russet burbank potatoes are an excellent source of fibre and potassium, and also provide good amounts of iron, folate, and vitamins C and B6.

Wondering how best to enjoy your russet burbank potatoes? We recommend using them to make this crispy hasselback potato gratin recipe, the perfect, comforting and hearty accompaniment to your meals, and these fluffy mashed potatoes, a heavenly dish!

We'd also recommend making classic russet burbank fries - the recipe is below!

Ingredients

  • 1kg russet burbank potatoes
  • 2.5L rapeseed oil
  • Sea salt

Method

  1. Keeping the skin on the potatoes, cut lengthways into 0.5cm thick discs and then cut these into 0.5cm thick sticks.
  2. Soak the raw fries in cold water for 20 minutes to remove some of the starch, drain and rinse with fresh water. Set aside to dry.
  3. Meanwhile, in a large pan heat the oil over medium heat to approx 160°C. Add a third of the potatoes and cook for 2-3 minutes, stirring occasionally until they soften.

Name: Potato - wilja
Description:
Wilja potatoes are divinely delicious all-rounder potatoes that are seriously underrated!
First cultivated in 1967 in the Netherlands, wilja potatoes are starting to be grown around the world - we source ours from Kent! These delectable potatoes are small to medium in size and round to oval in shape, and have visually appealing golden skin that's delicate and easy to peel. However, these potatoes are extremely versatile, being the perfect ingredient in any recipe calling for potatoes! Like other potatoes, wilja potatoes are an excellent source of dietary fibre and potassium, and also provide good amounts of iron, folate, and vitamins C and B6.

Name: Potato - yukon gold
Description:
Although first developed in Canada and named after the country's Yukon River, Yukon Gold potatoes are today one of the most popular potato varieties in the world - they were even the preferred potato of The Obamas when they were in the White House!
Yukon Gold potatoes are medium to large in size and have a slightly flatter shape than other varieties. Beneath their delicate, speckled, golden skin is golden-yellow flesh that is firm and moist. When cooked, Yukon Gold potatoes take on a creamy and tender consistency that delights the tastebuds: their melt-in-the-mouth flesh astounds with its buttery, earthy flavour, especially because they boast distinctive notes of sweetness.
These potatoes can be consumed in any way you'd eat other potato varieties, from roasting and baking to mashing and boiling. Did you know that they were the potato of choice for the dauphinoise at the state dinner, and that 600 kilograms of Yukon Gold potatoes were also used at the Oscars award show in 2016 where Wolfgang Puck served the tubers with crème Fraiche and Caspian caviar? They are particularly favoured by chefs because they retain their eye-catching golden hue even when cooked! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for a recipe for divine garlic mashed potatoes!
As well as being delicious and versatile, Yukon Gold potatoes are an excellent source of vitamin C - they contain nearly twice as much vitamin C as a regular baking potato! - are rich in dietary fibre and potassium, and provide a good amount of calcium.

Wondering how best to enjoy your Yukon Gold potatoes? Try the recipe below!

Recipe Suggestion - Garlic Yukon Gold Mashed Potato

Ingredients
- 900g yukon gold potatoes, washed and quartered
- 4 cloves garlic
- salt
- 350ml double cream, warm
- 110g butter, cold


Method
Place the potatoes and garlic in a large saucepan. Cover with 1 to 2 inches of cold water and season generously with salt. The water should taste like the sea. Taste it! 
If the water is under-seasoned at this point, it will be hard to have a well seasoned end product. 
Bring the pot of water to a boil and cook until the potatoes are fork-tender, about 20 to 25 minutes. Drain the potatoes and garlic well. 
Bring the heavy cream to a boil in a small saucepan. Once the cream has come to a boil remove from the heat. 
While the potatoes are still hot, add a third of the cream and butter then stir vigorously into the potatoes. Repeat this process two more times until all the cream and butter has incorporated. 
Taste the potatoes for seasoning and add salt, if needed. 
Serve immediately or cover with foil and keep warm in the oven on a low heat.

Name: Prekese
Description:
Prekese are hard brown pods with 4 ridges, which are native to Western Africa and mostly found in Ghana. The name is derived from Prks, aka Soup Perfume, as its sweet fragrance is highly prized and used to flavour soups. The fragrance is similar to that of carob.
One of its most common uses is to spice Banga soup which is a type of palm fruit soup. It's also used in pepper soup and in Ghana, soft drinks have been flavoured with this versatile fruit.
The fruit is regularly used as a dietary supplement rich in vitamins. The therapeutic properties of the plant have been documented since 1948 and authenticated in laboratory and field experiments.
Prekese is rich in protein, lipids, potassium, iron, magnesium, phosphorous, and vitamin C.

Name: Prekese
Description:
Prekese are hard brown pods with 4 ridges, which are native to Western Africa and mostly found in Ghana. The name is derived from Prks, aka Soup Perfume, as its sweet fragrance is highly prized and used to flavour soups. The fragrance is similar to that of carob.
One of its most common uses is to spice Banga soup which is a type of palm fruit soup. It's also used in pepper soup and in Ghana, soft drinks have been flavoured with this versatile fruit.
The fruit is regularly used as a dietary supplement rich in vitamins. The therapeutic properties of the plant have been documented since 1948 and authenticated in laboratory and field experiments.
Prekese is rich in protein, lipids, potassium, iron, magnesium, phosphorous, and vitamin C.

Name: Quince
Description:
Quinces are a must-try for all exotic fruit lovers!
Originating from Turkestan and Persia, quinces are now grown all over Europe.
Although raw quinces are inedible, they are nevertheless renowned - they are highly regarded for their aroma, upheld as superb natural air fresheners. Try leaving a quince in the glove box of your car and benefit from the wonderful fragrance for many months!
However, they offer more than an intense aroma! Known as 'apple' or 'pear' quinces depending upon their shape, the skin of these medium to large-sized fruits ripens to an eye-catching golden yellow. Beneath their appealing skin is dense cream to yellow coloured flesh that is astringent and sour but, once cooked, gains a delicious floral flavour with notes of honey! Indeed, quince is a highly prized fruit in Spain due to the popularity of 'membrillo', the delectable quince paste that results from boiling the fruits with sugar! After boiling, it is cooled, cut into squares and served with soft cheeses or as a candy.
Despite being best suited for making jams, preserves, pastes, and jellies, which pair wonderfully with poultry, beef and game, quinces are also perfect ingredients when making baked goods such as cakes and are also often infused with spirits including vodka and grappa! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including a scrumptious quince crumble tart!
As well as being versatile, quinces are nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre and provide a good amount of vitamin C and potassium.

Name: Safou
Description:
Want to try a fruit that has a taste comparable to a unique combination of green olive and avocado? Then you need to try safou!
These nutritious fruits native to West and Central Africa are typically small to medium in size and elongated in shape. They immediately catch the eye with their attractive, glossy, purple to bluish/black skin.
Beneath their smooth skin is soft flesh which varies in colour, ranging from green and brownish/cream to shades of pink. As well as wowing with its tender texture and citrus-like fragrance, the flesh astounds with its versatility: when eaten fresh, it has a wonderfully acidic flavour, whereas when it's roasted or quickly boiled in salted water, the pulp separates from the skin and long, brown, central seed and takes on a more gentle tangy, nutty flavour and an amazingly buttery texture. With the nickname 'butterfruit', it's not surprising that the flesh is velvety smooth!
Due to the mellower flavour and melt-in-the-mouth texture, safou is traditionally eaten cooked. It is typically eaten as a snack between meals, however in Nigeria, cooked safou pulp is combined with starchy foods like maize to make a hearty main course! Once the seed has been removed, you can stuff the fruit with cooked meats, spices, and vegetables for a real taste sensation, or why not try pureeing the pulp into a dip to serve with crisps and chips? Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some more recipe inspiration, including delectable roast tomatoes with safou!
Like its namesake butter, safou is high in fats and very calorie-dense. However, safou boasts nutritional benefits too: it has a high content of amino acids, the chemical building blocks of proteins, and is rich in potassium, calcium, and magnesium.

Name: Santol 'wild mangosteen'
Description:
If you love mangosteens then you need to try santol, the 'wild mangosteen' native to Cambodia, Laos, and Malaya!
Santols are small, round to oval-shaped fruits with golden yellow peel that is fuzzy and leathery, comparable to the skin of a peach. When you look beneath their wrinkled skin, you will understand why santol is also known as the 'cotton fruit' - they have wonderfully fluffy white flesh that is soft, spongy, and juicy. As with mangosteens, the flesh of santols never entirely separates from the internal, inedible seeds that it surrounds. Sucking the flesh provides an astounding sweet-sour flavour that delights the tastebuds, with their milky, creamy, sweetish juice being offset by tart, floral, and citrus notes! The ratio of sweet to sour varies depending upon the variety: the sweetest santol fruit has a sugary savour, with undertones of apple and peach, whilst a sour santol provides a distinctive umami flavour.
Although best enjoyed when simply eaten fresh out of hand, santols are also well-suited to a range of culinary applications. Description:
Sapote is a small to medium sized fruit with a thick, tough brown rind and bright orange flesh.
The flesh is fibrous but provides a delicious fruity flavour with hints of mango. To enjoy the flesh, it's best to suck it away from the fibres and this is why the fruit is known as 'chupa chupa' in Portuguese, which translates to suck suck!
It shares similarities with the mamey sapote but has a fruitier flavour and more fibrous flesh.

Name: Chilli - scotch bonnet
Description:
Scotch bonnets are a must-try for those looking for a way to add a kick of heat to their mealtimes!
Scotch bonnets are a variety of chilli pepper native to West Africa. They are small in size - average 2-7cm in length - and squat and wrinkled in shape. They have smooth, waxy skin that ripens from green to a vibrant red. Beneath their skin is crisp flesh encasing a cavernous hollow filled with small, flat cream-coloured seeds.
These brilliant peppers have a sweet aroma and a divinely floral, fruity savour with delectable undertones of cherry, tomatoes, and apples! After being delighted by these heavenly flavours, your tastebuds will be wowed by the intense fiery power of peppers, which boast a heat rating of 100,000-350,000 Scoville units! It's no wonder they are also known as 'Jamaican hots'!
Our maroon and deeply wrinkled dried scotch bonnets (packed in 40g bags) are similarly fiery, although the heat from these dried peppers tends to be less immediate and lingers for longer on the palette. They are particularly noted for their smoky savour, imbued with hints of spice and tropical undertones. They can be used in place of the fresh peppers: they are especially perfect for adding heat to raw dishes such as ceviches and their warm, fruity taste works well in combination with mangoes and berries. They also work well when added whole to curries and stews, but make sure to remove them before serving!
Many people will find the fresh peppers too hot to eat by themselves, preferring instead to add a small quantity to their cooking. Indeed, they are staple peppers in Caribbean cooking. They are perfect for boiling, sautéing, and frying, and work especially well when combined into curries, soups, and stews. They are also popularly used to make hot sauces - in Jamaica, they are favoured ingredients for making their famous spicy jerk seasoning! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including wonderful grilled jerk shrimp and pineapple skewers!
As well as being versatile, our 100% natural fresh, dried, and frozen scotch bonnets are also nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are excellent sources of vitamins A and C and magnesium and provide good amounts of flavonoids and phytochemicals.

Our dried seasoning peppers are washed, halved and dehydrated. There are no added ingredients. Add the dried seasoning peppers to your stews, curries and stir fries.

Name: Sea grapes
Description:
Grown in the seas around Vietnam, sea grapes - they owe their name to the fact they resemble bunches of very small green grapes - are popular throughout Asia, but in recent years have found particular favour in Japan, where they are called umibudo.
Also known as 'green caviar' due to their caviar-like appearance, sea grapes are actually a type of seaweed. Don't let that put you off though! Their salty flavour gives them real depth and they have an incredibly satisfying crunchy texture, with the tiny bubbles popping in your mouth as you bite them.
We offer two types of sea grapes: 20g sachets of dehydrated sea grapes and 20g packets of wet sea grapes. Our dehydrated sea grapes offer all the flavour and versatility of wet sea grapes and also boast a longer shelf-life, so they're the best choice if you want to enjoy them for longer.
Both are sure to wow your tastebuds though! Sea grapes are usually eaten raw once they've been soaked in and rinsed with water - follow the instructions on the packet (also listed in the preparation and usage sections below) to make sure you prepare and use them correctly.
After preparation, they are perfect for incorporating into a variety of dishes, from salads to sushi, rice, and noodles! They pair particularly well with wasabi and sesame sauces. However you use them, they will definitely bring freshness and a notable textural contrast to your meals!
As well as this, they are rich in fibre and contain an array of other healthful nutrients and minerals too, including calcium, iron, and magnesium.

Name: Soursop branches
Description:
Looking for a new herbal tea to try? Our 100% pure soursop branches from St Lucia are the ideal ingredient for you to buy!
Whilst exotic fruit lovers know all about the culinary applications of the soursop fruit and (to a lesser extent) its leaves, what is much less known is that the branches of the soursop tree can be used too!
Across Asia, soursop branches are, like the fruit and the leaves, believed to contain goodness. They are thus infused with boiling water to create a calming herbal tea, which is thought to possess beneficial medicinal properties.
The recipe could not be simpler. Simply let 3-5 branches infuse in boiling water for around 3 minutes, then remove. We think it is best consumed without milk, however you may want to add a natural sweetener such as honey.

Name: Soursop candied
Description:
Our candied soursop, also known mt mãng cu xiêm, is produced in Vietnam and is traditionally shared as a gift along with other candied fruits around lunar new year.
It's a delicious snack and popular among the Vietnamese especially during Tet when there is a popular adage: 'Eat sweet things and think sweet thoughts to ensure a fabulous year lies ahead'.
It's simply made using soursop and sugar. The flesh is removed from the seeds and skin then mixed with sugar. It's heated to dissolve the sugar and form a thicker texture then sealed in a wrapper and left to set.

Name: Soursop fruit powder (100% pure)
Description:
Our soursop fruit powder is made by dehydrating then finely grinding the flesh of mature semi-ripe soursop fruits.
The powder is intended to be used as a healthy supplement which can either be sprinkled onto various types of foods like yoghurt or cereal, added into numerous foods like ice ceam and cakes or finally mixed with water or milk to make a drink.
Just like our dried soursop and soursop crunch, the soursop fruit powder is 100% pure too so you can be comfortable in knowing that you're consuming only pure fruit. No nasty chemicals, preservatives, flavourings or sweeteners are added!
In order for our soursop fruit powder to be made without binding agents or any other chemicals we have to use fresh fruits which are only semi-ripe. If you attempt to make soursop fruit powder with fully ripe fruits the resulting powder is sticky and clumps together, it's not a smooth, dry powder.
People like this for its purity. Whilst using semi-ripe fruit means we can produce a smooth dry powder it means we can't capture the full flavour of fully ripe fresh soursop. This powder is lightly sweet.
For a soursop product that captures the flavour of the fresh soursop fruit you should definitely try our dried soursop. It's soft, sweet, chewy and delicious!
If you want to incorporate soursop into your diet and benefit from its nutritional properties then our soursop fruit powder is perfect for you. Conveniently packed in small packets you can either take this in your bag and make a drink / sprinke on your cereal when you arrive at work or you may prefer to purchase our bulk packs and enjoy regularly at home.

Name: Soursop, sarsaparilla, and sea moss teabags
Description:
Looking for a herbal tea with a difference? We think you'll be hard-pressed to find a more distinctive tea than our soursop, sarsaparilla, and sea moss tea!
Each of the wonderful ingredients in this tea are true Caribbean favourites:
Soursop, also known as graviola, guanabana, and guyabano, is perhaps the most well-known of the three. The spiky green fruit has become renowned not only for its amazing flavour - the flesh has hints of pineapple, strawberry, coconut, and banana! - but also for its perceived medical benefits.
Sea moss is a type of seaweed found along the coastlines of many of the world's continents. The sea moss hand-extracted from the Caribbean sea and then sun-dried is particularly favoured for its superior quality and flavour!
Sarsaparilla is a tropical plant that's been used in herbal medicines for millennia. The name is perhaps most recognised today as that of a popular soft drink - the drink known as sarsaparilla was commonly used as a home remedy and was also served in bars, however it's believed now that the drink was actually made from another plant, sassafras!
Combined, these three jewels of the Caribbean come together to make a splendid tropical drink! Simply brew one of the conveniently-packed teabags in a cup of boiling water for 1-2 minutes, and then your tea will be ready!
As well as being packed with flavour, this tea boasts many nutritional benefits. It's 100% natural, containing no additives, preservatives, or flavourings, and will add 0 calories and 0g of sugar to your diet!

Name: Star gooseberry
Description: Star gooseberries are a unique tropical fruit, recognised for their distinctive ribbed shape and refreshing sweet-tart flavour. Name: Stinking toe
Description:
The fruit of the West Indian locust tree may just win the award for the most unappealing nickname given to a fruit! It's nickname, 'stinking toe' is not without reason however, the pods are toe-shaped and some say the flesh inside stinks like feet. Much like the notorious durian fruit though, the smell of stinking toe is regarded as 'love it or hate it' so just as many people are fond of it as dislike it. Fortunately, the outer shell of the stinking toe is very hard, keeping the majority of the odour at bay until it's cracked with a strong knife or hammer.
Stinking toe matures during the rainy seasons and is then harvested during summer months. The presence of an unusual odour is actually a sign of ripeness.
The dry powdery cream coloured pulp, which resembles flour or icing sugar, has a sweet taste - some people say it tastes like dried milk. The miniature soluble fibers dissolve easily in water or milk, which it naturally thickens.
Whilst it can be enjoyed raw, it's often used in baking, blending, or cooking.
In Jamaica, where the fruit grows wild, locals blend the pulp with water, sugar, and spices to make a refreshing beverage.
In Brazil, where the fruit is known as jatobá, bakers use the dried powder of the pulp to make a biscuit-like pastry known as a broinha.
Stinking toe is considered one of the richest natural foods in the plant kingdom because of its high concentration of starches and proteins. Throughout Central and South America, the fruit is prized for its purported medicinal benefits. Its rumored to be everything from an aphrodisiac to a remedy for diarrhea.
The seeds are dispersed with the help of the agouti, a tropical rodent with teeth strong enough to break open the pods. They often carry the fruits to other areas and bury them for later. Forgotten fruits germinate and grow into new trees. It's thanks to the agouti, that stinking toe is now found throughout much of the Caribbean, Central America, and South America.

Name: Stone apple (bael)
Description:
Bael is an amazing fruit that has long been used in South Asian cuisine!
Round to oval in shape and small to medium in size, the bael fruit, also known as bilva, has a thick, hard, grey, green or yellow shell which takes some effort to crack. Indeed, the outer shell is so tough that the fruit has gained the nickname 'stone apple'!
However, the delicious flesh underneath is well worth the effort! After prizing open the shell, you are first greeted with a glorious floral aroma (it has been described as smelling of roses!), a fragrance resembling a unique combination of peach, lime, and passion fruit. Biting into the yellowish-brown flesh, filled with many small seeds, you will find that it is quite sticky, pasty, and extremely fibrous. The flavour of bael is unique: people have variously described it as sweet, astringent, fruity, and woody, with undertones of passionfruit, caramel, and tamarind; as its botanical name, aegle marmelos, hints at, the flavour is commonly likened to marmalade! In our opinion, though, we'd say the taste is comparable to egg fruit with a citrus edge. The delectable flesh also contains some pockets of clear sap, which tastes like a natural sugar syrup with notes of citrus.
Although most commonly eaten fresh, stone apples are also well suited to a number of culinary applications, from sprinkling onto your morning porridge or added into smoothies, pressed and strained into a refreshing juice (traditionally poured over ice), made into delightful chutneys and jams, and much more!
Stone apples are greatly valued in many Asian cultures for their nutritional properties, being, in particular, an excellent source of vitamins C and A and rich in fibre, calcium, and iron. As well as being eaten raw, the fruit is also commonly incorporated into natural medicines - for example, it is very popular to use immature bael fruits to make a digestion-enhancing juice by simply roasting the flesh and then pureeing it with water and sugar.

Sugar palm fruit looks somewhat like a whole young coconut but has a deep, blackish purple-coloured skin and 3 or 4 green leaves covering the top. When the fruit is ripe, the skin under the green leaves will be a bright orange colour.
More often, the sugar palm fruit is eaten whilst young when the outer husk is still unripe and the jelly seeds are the edible part. See: sugar palm fruit (young) https://www.myexoticfruit.com/shop/#!/products/sugar-palm-fruit
However, if the entire fruit is left to ripen, the outer husk of the palm fruit develops a delicious sweet flavour and is suitable to be eaten raw. The sweet pulp, which is grated or scraped away from the fibre is commonly used to make desserts and confectionery in South Asia.

Name: Tamarillo - amber
Description:
Having become increasingly popular in recent years due to their unique flavour and nutritional benefits, tamarillo are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
These small fruits resemble eggs in both size and shape. They have thin, glossy skin that has - as its name suggests - an attractive amber hue and once ripe, emit a wonderful floral aroma. Beneath this smooth peel is a layer of dense golden flesh surrounding juicy orange pulp that will wow your tastebuds with its glorious savour: the tender pulp boasts a rich sweet-savoury flavour that has been described as reminiscent of 'smokey spiced tomato'! The amber variety has a slightly milder flavour than other tamarillos but they are still delicious! The pulp also encases several small seeds which are not eaten.
The best way to enjoy tamarillos is to simply slice the fruits in half and scoop out the central pulp (the fruits are not eaten whole as the skin is extremely bitter). However, the pulp's umami flavour means it is also well-suited to a range of culinary applications. We'd particularly recommend soaking the pulp in sugar and then serving it with everything from cereal and yoghurt to ice cream and tarts! Tamarillos also make divine jams, jellies, and salsas and can be added to soups and stews. In South America, it is common to blend tamarillos into smoothies and to pickle them into tangy condiments. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some recipe inspiration, including a splendid tamarillo hot sauce!
Our dried tamarillo slices are similarly delicious and versatile. Dried tamarillos are similar to sun-dried tomatoes, although the tamarillos contain notably less moisture. The chewy dried slices can be enjoyed as a tangy snack, ground into seasoning, or added to sauces!
As well as being supremely delectable, tamarillo are nutritionally valuable. In particular, they are an excellent source of vitamins A and C and provide a good amount of dietary fibre. As our dried tamarillo are made from 100% pure fruit, they offer many of the same nutritional benefits as fresh tamarillo, and you can be confident in knowing that you're consuming only natural goodness, with no additives, colourings, or preservatives.

Name: Tamarind sour
Description:
Our sour tamarind is organically grown on a farm in St Lucia. It has a sour flavour, unlike tamarind commonly found in Southeast Asia which is sweet.
As well as being eaten as a snack, tamarind is also often used in cooking.
Tamarind has a unique flavour. The soft flesh that surrounds the shiny black seeds tastes like a mixture of dates and raisins. Some people also compare it to the flavour of 'Cola'.
To prepare tamarind for cooking, crack and remove the shell. Soak the pulp in warm water for 10 minutes. Mix it together and strain through a fine sieve. Throw away the pulp and use the liquid.

Name: Tamarind - velvet tamarind
Description:
Velvet tamarind is a fascinating fruit which is commonly found in Africa and in some parts of Southeast Asia.
It takes the name velvet tamarind because of the smooth, soft velvet-like exterior.
The small, thin pods are easily cracked to reveal a dry, powdery flesh which surrounds a small, shiny central seed.
The flesh is delicious and enjoyable to eat. Its flavour is like candy and has some resemblance to the more commonly found sweet tamarind (known as 'tamarindus indica').
The seeds and pod are not eaten.
Our velvet tamarind from Sri Lanka tends to be smaller than our other varieties. They have a thin layer of flesh that boasts a sweet-sour flavour, with the tangy notes usually dominating. If you're looking for sweeter fruits, we'd recommend our velvet tamarind from Nigeria.

Name: Tamarind - young
Description: Young tamarind is a prized tropical delicacy, loved for its crisp texture and refreshing sweet-tart flavour. Harvested before the pods fully mature, young tamarind has tender edible flesh with a milder taste than ripe tamarind, making it perfect for fresh eating and a variety of traditional dishes. Enjoy young tamarind as a snack on its own or add it to salads, stir-fries, curries, soups, and chutneys for a bright, tangy flavour. It is especially popular in Southeast Asian cuisine, where its fresh, zesty taste complements both savoury and spicy recipes. Naturally containing vitamin C, fibre, and beneficial antioxidants, young tamarind is a delicious way to add a tropical twist to your meals. The tender pods can be enjoyed fresh or incorporated into your favourite recipes.

Description: Tomatillos are a vibrant green fruit, often used as a vegetable in cooking, and are a staple ingredient in Mexican cuisine. Perfect for making authentic salsa verde, tomatillos can also be roasted, grilled, or blended into soups, sauces, curries, and stews. Naturally rich in vitamin C, fibre, and antioxidants, tomatillos are a nutritious addition to a balanced diet. Name: Turmeric
Description:
Looking for a way to add a kick of spice to your mealtimes? Our fresh turmeric is just the thing for you!
Fresh turmeric is elongated and slender in shape, somewhat resembling a long finger, and has brownish-orange skin that is thin, rough, and marked with wrinkles and knobs. Beneath this textured skin is eye-catching bright orange flesh that will wow your tastebuds with its delicious flavour: it has distinctive warming properties and wonderful peppery notes, with strong undertones of carrot and ginger. Did you know it is one of the ingredients that constitutes curry powder?
Although most often boiled and dried to create turmeric powder, fresh turmeric can also be fried and pickled, and is perfect for adding gentle freshness to curries. Its colour alone is enough to make turmeric a superior culinary ingredient - it is sure to brighten up any dish! Indeed, it is also known as 'Indian saffron' because it is often used in Indian cuisine as a substitute for saffron in bringing some visual vibrancy. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including an extremely healthy tropical turmeric smoothie!
As well as being versatile and delectable, turmeric also boasts many nutritional benefits. In particular, its primary active ingredient, curcumin, has powerful anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties that have made the spice popular in Chinese and Ayurvedic medicines for centuries.
We also have organic and fair trade turmeric from small-scale farmers deep in Peru.

Name: Wampee fruit
Description:
We doubt even our most knowledgeable exotic fruit connoisseurs have heard of the little-known wampee fruit!
Wampee fruits are the very small fruits of the wampee tree, an evergreen tree found most commonly in Southeast Asia. The fruits are oval in shape and have smooth, thin, golden-yellow skin. They are very similar in appearance to lychee, but are actually part of the citrus family!
Beneath this eye-catching skin is delicate and supremely succulent white flesh that has an enticing floral aroma and a divine sweetness that is complemented by pleasant sour notes. Within the flesh, there are several medium-sized seeds, which are typically discarded. The skin can be eaten though, and we'd recommend doing so, because otherwise you'll miss its spicy flavour!
Wampee are best enjoyed when simply eaten fresh out of hand. However, they are also well-suited to a number of culinary applications. When the skins are kept on, the fruits have a unique umami flavour that makes them ideal for sweet and savoury dishes. We'd particularly recommend cooking them with meat-based dishes and using them to make thirst-quenching drinks - look in the 'Further information' tab below for a recipe for a wampee fruit martini!

Description:
Waxberries, native to East Asia, are a delicious small crimson to dark purple coloured fruit with a sweet flavour and bumpy surface. Each fruit has a single seed in the centre which is discarded.

Name: Wood apple (kodbel)
Description:
A fruit that is considered so sacred in India that it is offered to the god Ganesh, wood apples are a must-try for exotic fruit lovers!
Wood apples are small to medium in size and round (often perfectly spherical) in shape. From the exterior they somewhat resemble small coconuts: they have an extremely hard, rough brown shell that needs to be hit firmly with the back of a cleaver to be cracked.
Beneath this tough shell is a surprising interior! The brown flesh inside showcases an array of textures due to its combination of seeds and long, stringy fibres - we'd describe the texture as creamy, moist, and slightly crunchy and grainy. The flavour is unique too, with the moist, sticky, and fibrous pulp combining sweet and savoury notes and musky undertones. We'd liken the savour to an unusual mix of tamarind, raisins, and cheese! Everything inside the shell is edible, however the fibres and seeds are discarded by some.
With a fragrance comparable to raisins and blue cheese and an unmatched flavour profile, it's safe to say that eating the flesh simply fresh out of hand is a real experience! However, for the best enjoyment of these wonderful fruits, we'd recommend using them to make delectable juices and chutneys, as is common in their native Sri Lanka and India - check out the 'Further information' tab below for a recipe for an amazing wood apple chutney! In Sri Lanka, wood apple flesh is popularly mixed with coconut milk and palm sugar to create a sweet, slightly acidic beverage that is an ideal thirst-quencher in hot weather. Indeed, they make spectacular fruity milkshakes and smoothies!
As well as being versatile, wood apples have long been a staple of Ayurvedic medicine, and they are still today consumed for their nutritional benefits. In particular, they are rich in dietary fibre and vitamin C and provide good amounts of calcium and iron.

Name: Yam - Chinese (grown in France)
Description:
Chinese yams are delicious vegetables that are full of healthful nutrients and vitamins!
Despite their name, we source these yams from France - yams have been grown on the banks of the River Loire for over 100 years! Beneath this thick, cylindrical vegetable's tough, brown skin is delectable, starchy white/cream-coloured flesh, that has an earthy, largely neutral, flavour - Chinese yams have slightly softer flesh than other yams, and are fresher rather than sweet in taste. When cooked, the earthy flavour is mellowed, and the taste becomes comparable to that of potatoes, with notes of chestnut.
Yams are staples of millions of people's cuisine, typically consumed in a similar fashion to how we consume potatoes in the UK. We too would recommend using them as you would usually use potatoes: you could make a gratin, with bechamel sauce and grated cheese; superb French fries, and mash or roast them. There are so many ways to use these versatile vegetables! They are a perfect way of adding texture to soups, stews, and casseroles, and their mild taste means they are also excellent at soaking up the flavour of spices. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for some of our favourite recipes, including wonderful Cantonese pork soup with yam and carrots!
Additionally, Chinese yams boast a range of nutritional benefits. Used for centuries in traditional medicine, they are still today vaunted as excellent sources of dietary fibre, and are also highly regarded for their richness in iron, calcium, potassium, and vitamin B1.

Name: Yam - cush
Description:
Cush yams are delicious vegetables that are full of healthful nutrients and vitamins!
Beneath the tough, brown skin of these thick, cylindrical vegetables from Brazil is delectable, starchy white/cream-coloured flesh, that has an earthy, largely neutral, flavour, tinged with a subtle sweetness - when cooked the earthy flavour is mellowed in favour of a stronger, but still mellow, sweetness, and the taste becomes comparable to that of potatoes, with notes of chestnut.
Just as puna yams grown in Africa are staples of the continent's cuisine, so cush yams cultivated across South America are common features in a range of dishes in countries such as Brazil, Peru, and Ecuador. With a flavour similar to potatoes, we would recommend using them as you would usually use potatoes: boiling, frying, mashing, and roasting are the most common ways of enjoying these yams. Whereas other yams have only a mild flavour, the smooth, moist flesh of cush yams boasts an unexpectedly rich taste, making them ideal ingredients in cooking! Check out the 'Further information' tab below for a recipe for sopa de cara, a deliciously creamy soup popular in Brazil!
Like other yams, cush yams are not only an excellent source of dietary fibre, but they are also rich in vitamins C and B1, and provide good amounts of potassium and magnesium.

Name: Yam - white
Description:
White yams are delicious vegetables that are cultivated in many parts of the world, primarily in countries in Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean.
Beneath white yams' brown skin is an appetizing, starchy, fibrous white flesh, which has an earthy, largely neutral, flavour, tinged with a very faint sweetness - the flavour is comparable to that of potatoes. Indeed, in the regions they hail from they are in a similar fashion to how we consume potatoes in the UK, and have thus long been a staple food in Asian, African, and Caribbean cuisine. Their mild taste means they are excellent at soaking up the flavour of spices.
It is their nutritional benefits, however, that really entice people to eat white yams. Not only are they an excellent source of dietary fibre, but they are also rich in various minerals, including potassium and magnesium, several antioxidants, and have a high content of a unique, naturally-occurring compound called 'diosgenin', which is believed to boost intellectual functions such as memory.
As aforementioned, white yams are usually consumed like potatoes, so boiling, frying and roasting are the most common ways of cooking them. Check out the 'Further information' tab below for recipes on how to make a delicious white yam stew and some traditional 'pounded yam' to accompany it?

It is their nutritional benefits, however, that really entice people to eat white yams. Name: Mango - mallika

Mallika are a rare mango highly prized for their sweetness.
Mangoes from India are regarded by many as some of the best mangoes in the world, and mallika are no exception.
A result of hybridisation between dasheri and neelam mangoes, mallika are a medium to large variety with an elongated shape and green-yellow skin that ripens to a golden yellow. Beneath smooth skin is dark orange flesh that is dense, fibreless and succulent around a small slender seed. These mangoes have a fruity, floral aroma that is characteristic of mangoes from South Asia, and their flavour is equally superb. Although mallika mangoes are best enjoyed fresh out of hand, they are also great for use in any number of food and drink recipes. Due to their honey-like taste, they are particularly perfect when complimenting sweet dishes. Wed recommend using them to make desserts such as tarts, puddings, sorbets and ice cream. Why not respect their Indian roots by pureeing and mixing the mangoes with milk or cream and then using it as a delicious dipping sauce?
As well as being brilliantly appetizing mangoes boast a range of nutritional benefits too. In particular, they are an excellent source of dietary fibre, are rich in vitamins A and C, and provide a good amount of magnesium and potassium.
